speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ORDER OF BUSINESS TO BE CONSIDERED THIS DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought it would be helpful to hon. members if I were to take a moment to outline the government's intentions regarding the program for today's sitting. In an effort to do this I should indicate to hon. members that they will notice on today's order paper under government notices of motions a motion to amend the terms of reference of the joint committee dealing with consumer credit so that committee will be instructed "also to inquire into and report upon the trends in the cost of living in Canada and factors which may have contributed to changes in the cost of living in Canada in recent months." Some reference was made to this motion last night in the speech of the Minister of Finance. I believe that motion in the normal course of business will be transferred under standing order 21 (2) to orders of the day for consideration later this day or at the next sitting. I believe that is the form.
This motion could be called when we come to orders of the day, and it could be debated and carried on the understanding that immediately that is done we would call the estimates of the Department of Finance and continue our discussion of the estimates, as was done yesterday. Or we could call the estimates first and then consider the motion later in the day.
We also have to put the formal motion for adjournment, which is in the precise terms of the motion carried on July 14. Perhaps I can refresh the minds of hon. members by indicating that that motion read, in part, in this way: "that when this house adjourns at the end of the ... this ... sitting it shall stand adjourned until Wednesday, October 5, at 2.30 o'clock p.m.". Then there was the proviso about an earlier calling back should that be necessary. That motion will require to be put at some time, and if it is agreeable I propose to move it when we reach motions in our proceedings today.
I am open to suggestions from other house leaders or other hon. members as to what disposition we should make of the other notice of motion to which I referred, the notice of motion enlarging the terms of reference of the committee to investigate the rising cost of living. If hon. members prefer to discuss the estimates first, that would be of no concern to the government. I think any matter that can be discussed under the one item can be discussed under the other, but I am open to suggestions as to which one hon. members would wish to have called first.
That is the way, Mr. Speaker, that we propose to proceed today, and I thought it useful to put this statement on the record at this time so that hon. members would be clear as to the program we have in mind for today's sitting of the house.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CANADIAN ATTITUDE TOWARD ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the United Nations will have been convened before we meet again, provided the motion for adjournment is accepted later this day, will the minister now say on behalf of the government of Canada what the attitude of the government is going to be on the

question of the seating of communist China in the United Nations? In that connection, what is the government's stand in respect of Formosa and the necessity of assuring that that government and people will not be sacrificed in consequence of any action taken?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secrefary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN ATTITUDE TOWARD ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the general assembly will open on September 20. The question of mainland China's admission to the United Nations will not be disposed of or dealt with until some time later during the assembly, very likely some time around the end of November. The position of Canada with regard to universality of membership has been stated and reaffirmed by me in the general assembly. We strongly support the position taken by the secretary general that the principle of universality should be observed. To this end we expressed the view last year that we would hope it would be possible for all sovereign bodies to take their places in the United Nations.
The question of Formosa does not present a problem in this regard. It is not the intention of the government of Canada to deny the right of 12 million people in Formosa to participate in the world body. We continue to express the hope that the conditions laid down by mainland China for admission, as stated by her foreign minister Chen Yi on September 29 last, will not be raised again this year. There will be an opportunity later during the session, in the light of events, to say more about this matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CANADIAN ATTITUDE TOWARD ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
Has there been any
change in the attitude of the minister that communist China should be admitted, as he was reported to have stated on August 15 at Banff? Has there been any change in that attitude since then? In particular, has there been any change in relation to the fact that, as the minister then stated, no acceptable means of bringing communist China into the United Nations has been offered or, indeed, has seemed possible?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN ATTITUDE TOWARD ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
No, there has been no change in that statement. It was made after the most careful consideration. I would hope that if there is any solution to this it might be put forward by interested countries with which we are having consultations. There can be no doubt as to the view of the Canadian government, having regard to the serious situation in the world, of the
September 9, 1966
desirability of participation in the United Nations by all sovereign states.
If a way can be found to meet the principle of universality in this situation we would wish to do so. In stating this we are taking into consideration the position of countries with which we have close association, and I do not refer only to the United States; I refer also to Australia, to New Zealand, to Japan, to countries in Asia and to other countries which feel that in the interests of world peace this problem of the admission of China to the United Nations should be resolved.

Mr. Chairman, I started last
night to give my impression from the standpoint of an independent member in this house and you will agree that it can be different from the opinion expressed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and from certain comments made by the spokesmen of the opposition parties.
I said that, in my opinion, the minister's speech appeared to me as a courageous diagnosis which, for instance, a surgeon would make after examining a patient and finding out that his condition is getting worse. And the diagnosis is all the more courageous because the minister admitted that the condition of the patient-Canada or the Canadian economy in the circumstances-became worse these last five months, when he had anticipated that it would improve.
I added, Mr. Chairman, that the problem of inflation is a rather complex matter, that it seemed to me that the minister is quite qualified to suggest cures, since he has at his disposal a whole team of experts and he has had himself a wide experience in government matters, in short, that he is always in consultation with financial experts from all over the

world with whom we have financial connections.
And I think I could say as much if we had a Conservative government, because I presume that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) would have tried to choose as head of that department a competent man who could benefit also from the same advice of experienced people.
Mr. Chairman, I added that I had a lot
more confidence in the minister's directives, precisely because of his qualifications, than in some remedies-which remind me of quacks' or old wives' remedies-proposed by some hon. members who cannot offer the same qualifications.
Mr. Chairman, it was said during this debate that the government was probably to blame for inflation. The public was thus given the impression that Canada is the only country faced with inflation, and yet it is raging throughout the world. One has only to read a financial publication to find evidence thereof. For instance, in the September 2 issue of Time there is an article which reads as follows:

In West Germany, credit is so tight that Frankfurt last week cancelled plans to build a new subway system, while Dusseldorf was forced to call off construction of a new city hall, auditorium and athletic stadium.

You will note, Mr. Chairman, that those are countries which are reputed for their solid financial structure and which do not indulge in fantasy.

In Switzerland, commercial banks last month raised the prime interest rate from 5 per cent to 6 per cent, the first such increase since 1937 in the frugal little country.
In Sweden, the shortage of loan funds is such that high-priority apartment construction in Stockholm has been cut back 40 per cent, and the average wait for an apartment is now ten years.
In Norway, big and small businesses this summer are getting bleak answers when they make loan applications as longtime bank customers: "Sorry, but we don't have money."
In Britain, banks are now within 1 per cent, or $47,500,000 of the ceiling on the amount of money that they can lend;

And it continues along the same lines, and we note, Mr. Chairman, that the same situation prevails in all the countries of the world. Even the U.S. which is supposed to be a
September 9, 1966

leader in the financial field is faced with problems. This was evidenced this morning in the statement of President Johnson, who must take austerity measures concerning industry and high finance-fortunately-rather than against the small people.
Again in the September 9 issue of Time we read that even Wall Street financiers urge the government to take emergency action, and I quote on page 79 from the section entitled- [English]
Ordinarily, talk about higher taxes is not very cheery. But U.S. stock and bond investors last week seemed to brighten up just when word got out that the Johnson administration was seriously considering tax increases as an adjunct to tight money in the fight against inflation.
[DOT] (12 noon)

This disease is common not only to Canada, but to the whole world. In every country, you have all kinds of governments: conservatives, liberals, democrats, republicans, and I believe the most affected country is England whose government is closely related to our New Democratic Party. We will not put the blame on any individual, any party, because it is a general disease, and so we must have the courage to take the necessary measures to prevent this disease from spreading and bringing on disaster.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I come to certain conclusions. I believe all Canadians should be reassured for two reasons: the first is that today's governments are prepared to deal with the situation, to prevent it from turning into a catastrophe, because we have experts today who are able to make financial forecasts and counsel governments, so that these governments may take the necessary steps when it is time. I repeat that, in this matter, I have full confidence in the hon. Minister of Finance.
There is also a second reason. We now have in Canada social legislation providing our economy with hundreds of millions of dollars, if not over a thousand million each year, which helps to stabilize the Canadian economy. But in spite of all this, strong measures will have to be taken. I will say only this to the hon. Minister of Finance: In the measures you are going to take, do your utmost to spare the small wage-earner, the one who lives with austerity the year round.
Let us not take away the butter on his bread, for pity's sake, and let us endeavour to impose austerity onto those who have the means to pay, the financiers, manufacturers, and businessmen who can always make out,
Supply-Finance
and let us go as easy as possible on the wage-earners, particularly the low wage-earners.
And I will now point out to the hon. minister it is time to remember that this government has been accused of indecision, procrastination and weakness in dealing with certain problems; so it is now time for the government to prove that it has the necessary determination to apply to the Canadian economy the measures necessary to put it back on its feet. The time has come to face this crisis bravely, to make all Canadians understand that an operation, never a pleasant thing, is absolutely necessary. No one is happy when his surgeon tells him that he will have to remove a vital part of his body, but when he learns that he will get worse and die unless he is operated on, he reconciles himself to that fact, and asks the surgeon to be quick.
I think the government will show courage and determination. It has all it needs to understand the situation. It must not let itself be impressed by the criticism of some irresponsible or inexperienced journalists, by some members of this house who are more interested in promoting the interests of their party than in working for the good of the Canadian economy. The minister would be wise to listen to some of the suggestions, because the members of the opposition have made some that are worthwhile, but I think he should concern himself only with constructive criticism. He should not let himself be dissuaded from the course of action he has taken. In the present situation, he should himself forget the political considerations of his own party, forget future elections, and believe that Canadians today are better informed than they have ever been, that they will not swallow anything and that they will not be bluffed. Canadians realize more than ever that a financial crisis does exist and they expect their government to come forward with remedies or cures, or even painful operations, to prevent the problem from becoming more serious.
Mr. Chairman, I have one last point to make and then I will resume my seat. Last evening, during the debate, an hon. member bluntly stated that I would probably go back to the Liberal party before too long. He might have meant it as an insult; I will simply remind this kind hon. member that I left the Liberal party of my own accord, that I am happy as an independent, that I can now say out loud what everybody thinks and says in a whisper, that I do not have to keep

silent for political reasons, that I can stand up and criticize the government when I conscientiously believe I should do so, but, on the other hand, I would be ill-advised and remiss in my responsibilities toward my constituents if I failed to recognize the good things accomplished by the government, to recognize especially that the government has certain responsibilities to discharge, and, also, if I did not give the government the support to which it is entitled, because, as an independent member, I do not work for the Liberal party but for Canada, for my province, for my constituency.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to commend the last speaker, the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) for the speech, full of wisdom and objectivity, he has just delivered, and also for his contribution to this most important problem.

I listened last night with great interest, Mr. Chairman, to the contributions that were made by two Conservative members, one N.D.P. member, the leader of the Ralliement party and the leader of the Social Credit party. I struggled to discover what was the conclusion of these hon. members to this inflationary problem that faces Canada and, as the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres has indicated, the entire western world. I was confused about this. It almost appears to me, sir, that we have forgotten somewhat the experience of the thirties. Certainly, during the time I have been a member in the last four parliaments we have shown considerable preoccupation with long and middle-run economic problems, problems relating to exchange and growth and distribution. But in so far as shorter term problems relating to cyclical fluctuation are concerned, it would appear that we have tended to forget them even though they were so much the concern of the pre-war generation in Canada.
The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi made a carefully prepared speech last evening. He spoke in terms of excessive interest rates. He spoke about the need to control inflation. Then he stated his fear that the minister had enunciated negative, short-term remedies to combat inflation and, in effect, urged the federal government to increase substantially its expenditures on such matters as retraining, housing, zoning, the ARDA program and so on. He spoke about the need for long-term measures to be taken to combat inflation. This was the burden of his remarks.

Actually it is difficult to find very much that was truly unique and different in the remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. He was derisive of the Minister of Finance for the financial measures adopted, which he argued were as old and as orthodox as fiscal and monetary policy could be. For my part I am very grateful for the fact that following the study of the commission on Canada's economic prospects, the royal commission of 1957 which addressed itself in the main to manpower, productivity and output, and the need for trained manpower and research, we have had two important studies by the Economic Council of Canada.
The first study related to economic goals for Canada by 1970. In December, 1965, there was the more searching and shorter term study which addressed itself to a sustained and balanced economic growth. I am grateful for the fact that we have as Minister of Finance a man uniquely qualified in graduate studies, first at Manitoba and later at London School of Economics; a man with practical experience having discharged important duties in the finance department and the Wartime Prices and Trade Board, a scholar who in 1947 became director of the economic policy division of the Department of Finance, who in 1955 and 1956 led important teams to negotiate trade agreements with Russia and Japan, basically in the field of food, who led many important deliberations for the western world in GATT, who in 1963 succeeded to the important portfolio of Trade and Commerce and then took over the watchdog duties of the Department of Finance. We must regard our Minister of Finance as the guardian of the nation. It is his duty to represent all of the people, and I would think in particular the consumer. We have in the minister a man who understands the machinery for fiscal controls at the government's command and knows how and when to use them.

What are the pressures with which we are faced? On March 21, 1966, the Minister of
September 9, 1966

Finance spoke honestly and frankly, just as he did last night. He said in part that our problem was not to put a brake on the economy but to see that we do not press too hard on the accelerator and throw the car off the road. If one gathers together the several speeches which have been made by the hon. gentleman in the field of balance of payments, in the field of exports and imports, in the field of growth, and now more particularly in the short-run area of cyclical theory, I think we have as fine a set of addresses on economic problems in Canada as we can find from any Minister of Finance who has ever held this portfolio. We have had good ministers of finance during periods of war and some during post-war periods, but not many have had the chance to assume different portfolios and responsibilities which cover the entire range of our economic problems.
In another address relating to the problem of poverty the Minister of Finance said that Canada's major problem in 1966 seems to be to restrain the economy from trying to expand more rapidly than physically possible. That was his conclusion of many months ago. In another address he indicated that prosperity tends to widen the gulf between the rich and the poor, just as depression tends to be a leveller. His advice to the nation was that we should proceed with discipline. In naval terms, we must advance line abreast, not line astern.
Some of the N.D.P. members seem to be uproarious in their laughter, but my contention is that regardless of where a man fits into society, whether he be an old age pensioner, a worker in a trade union, a school teacher, a clerk or doctor, even a person clipping coupons, there is essentially only one way in which the nation can advance and that is line abreast. It is ridiculous to suggest that simply by taxing away profits we can right this distortion of inflation, at the same time encouraging price increases in other directions.
The problems that are facing Canada are clearly understood by bankers, businessmen and economists, if not by some of the members of parliament.

speechtext:
No, but it is a useful intervention because we are getting some very able and responsible assistance from labour today on matters not entirely along the lines indicated by members of the opposition. I do not think that Canadians are so naive as to overlook the dangers with which we are currently faced.
This is the longest period of economic expansion in Canadian peacetime history. It has produced an extended series of annual increases in before-tax profits of corporations. In some instances the profits of certain corporations, perhaps those in a monopolistic or quasi-monopolistic position, have been so high that there has been, as in the case of the United States and as in the United Kingdom, the danger of high-profit industries being able to pay labour so well that they are more or less able to entice them away from other industries which are operating marginally, therefore increasing the danger of bottlenecks.
This year, though business activity continued to expand strongly, rising costs which are associated with an economy operating at levels closer to capacity than at any time for a decade were beginning to take their toll of profits. In the early months of this year in Canada and the United States business forged ahead at a rate that was clearly unsustainable. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle are apparently not interested in these facts.
It appears to me that cyclical theory now requires us to look through a microscope at the special problems of the top quarter of the upswing. If I can make an analogy, it seems to me that what we have to do is to exercise the art of riding a surfboard. If that can be done with skill, courage and aplomb, growth will quite conceivably continue onwards. Indeed, there may be many higher waves behind this wave and we do not need to be the helpless victims of circumstances. But for us to suggest or to think for one moment that this situation is something within the easy control of the Canadian government alone is specious and untrue.
The economies of both the United States and Canada have been operating at very close to capacity for several quarters and the signs of strain that had begun to appear in 1965 have become unmistakable. Therefore when we use the expression "overheating", that is a simple statement of fact.
Many records have been achieved in Canada this year as this high level of activity

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance
has increased. There is no doubt that the increase in real output, in spite of the many labour differences which have occurred, will be in the neighbourhood of 6 per cent. But the upward trend in prices and costs is causing concern. The consumer price index has risen by over 2 per cent in 1966 and the wage settlements negotiated so far this year have resulted in considerably larger wage increases than in previous years. So that we are facing a new plateau of higher prices and higher costs which is going to take some time to work its way through the economy. But these price increases may accelerate unless a determined effort is made to counteract the increasing inflationary pressures. The threat of inflation has increased, and this will weaken Canada's competitive position both at home and abroad.
I have been looking at the publication of
the Ontario Department of Economics and Development which is called "Ontario Economic Review". In its volume for April of this year there were 12 graphs. On these 12 graphs we find depicted an increase in business, industrial and engineering contracts in Ontario, in new orders for manufacturing in Canada and in wages and salaries in Ontario. Relatively, the consumer price index is flat; it shows a much more modest increase. Yet the gross national product is still increasing steadily, and this increase appears to be relatively higher than that shown by the consumer price index.
When we consider the combination of increasing prices, increasing wages and also the increase in investment capital, which is another factor in the rigidities and illiquidity which has developed, we are facing a major problem which must be met by these fiscal and monetary techniques.
In the May-June issue of the same publication of the Ontario Department of Economics and Development appears a report produced by Mr. H. Ian Macdonald, chief economist. He talks about construction contracts which are currently being awarded in Ontario and indicates that many large construction awards were recently placed in that province, all of which were for very valid purposes. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands thinks that there is no limit to this expansion. When I look at the construction which is being carried out, such as the Beaverton home for the aged, a building at Ottawa university, provincial highway projects, and so on, I commend them. I find myself much more enthused about hospital extensions than

I am about shopping centres and mail order buildings.
What is the effect of all this? The effect must be that if we do not accomplish greater co-operation with the provinces, particularly the industrialized provinces in central Canada, in pacing production, we shall fail by trying to do too much too quickly. That is the advice and guidance we have had from the minister and it is important that this advice should be followed. This I think, emphasizes the importance of the forthcoming dominion-provincial discussions with respect to the solving of such constitutional difficulties as may exist inhibiting action.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
Mr. Graham Towers points particularly to the matter of credit and says:
-I doubt that the pace of the recent credit expansion can be maintained without causing trouble.
He indicates to us that the gross national product in North America last year grew in excess of 9 per cent and, while price increases accounted for a portion of that, the real increase on a per capita basis was in the neighbourhood of 4J per cent. In other words, we are growing and we shall continue to grow, but we should not allow greed to push us over the brink.
It is easy, of course, to be a Liberal administration if you have opposition that comes from both the Conservative side of the house and from the New Democratic Party or socialist group-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: And also within your own party.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Perhaps I should say, from the Progressive Conservative party, in answer to the right hon. gentleman who interjected. It is easier to be a Liberal if you are going to move forward guided by advice from a side which supports some restraint. There are some who desire to conserve and there are others who have an enthusiastic interest to progress rapidly and to be as progressive as possible without any concern for restraint. We have not had in the twenty six and twenty seventh parliaments, certainly not in the twenty seventh parliament, any serious words of restraint.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Not from the opposition.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Not from the opposition. I think this is manifestly so. Certainly we have not had them from the first two Conservative speakers in this debate. Their emphasis is that it is only by further pump priming that
September 9, 1966

we can remove ourselves from our present difficulties.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Nor have you had any from the right wing of your cabinet.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: From the right wing?

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: From the chancery wing. From the old guard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: I have high regard for what people such as John Deutsch, Louis Rasmin-sky and Robert Bryce have to say. I have high regard for what the Minister of Finance, who is responsible and trying to be as fair and just as he can be under these circumstances, has to say, namely, that it is only by adopting certain disciplinary measures that remedies to inflation can be found.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: What does the Minister of National Health and Welfare say?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: John Meyer has warned us. I know the official opposition are not interested in his warning, but here we have a case where the mid-year survey of capital investment commitments by government shows that, despite a reduction of 4.9 per cent, they are still running at 8.9 per cent ahead of last year's expenditures. It is clear from the various articles that John Meyer has written that the progress in the first quarter of this year cannot possibly be expected to continue. There is such a thing as overheating, and one must take care of the economy. Certainly one sees the wisdom of looking after an engine. We have to consider the wisdom of looking after our our own industrial and financial situation in much the same way.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
I should prefer to carry on at this time. When I have finished I shall try to answer questions.
I might suggest to the Minister of Finance one excellent way in which $12 to $15 million could currently be saved. I think it might be worth while to examine the proposal with respect to the electrification of the Rideau canal and river system. This has been considered for some years and certainly engineering studies and advice exist. The proposed electrification is, I think, unnecessary and undesirable.
If I may refer to the wise remarks of the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, he indicated the universal character of the inflationary problem. At first blush many of us would be happy to consider bold and dramatic steps to
Supply-Finance
cope with the cost of living. The question we find continually raised in the United States and in Canada is whether wage and price controls should be implemented. A lot of thought has been given to this matter.
I note in the current issue of XJ.S. News and World Report that there is reference to pressures in late August and September and to government action to clamp down on the overheated boom in that country. They estimate in the United States that the boom has reached a critical stage, requiring the most careful handling. A sober analysis is given in U.S. News and World Report, which says that in the United States there is ahead a period of growing strain and mounting pressure, and that labour shortages, skilled and even unskilled, will grow more severe. Unemployment in the United States, now at 3.9 per cent of the work force, will slip to 3.5 per cent. I believe in Canada we are in the region of 3.5 per cent to 4 per cent. The report indicates that by the end of the year the United States figure will perhaps fall to 3.1 per cent. People generally and businessmen and politicians do not like controls, and short of an emergency such as a world war they do not work.
I was impressed by the column by Henry Wallich which appeared in the September 5 issue of Newsweek. It is headed: "Can We Stop Inflation Without A Recession?" He studies the question of direct price controls. He comes to the conclusion as a result of careful analysis of this problem that fiscal and monetary restraints are the only tools that can be relied on to do anything in the immediate future.
With reference to what the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi said last night, in Canada we are in a somewhat different position from the United States. We have a very limited constitutional power. The government may assume certain powers during a national emergency, but we do not at this time have the powers to step in to exercise the kinds of controls which have been referred to and which are clearly beyond federal jurisdiction. I do feel that continuing discussion with the provinces is of the greatest importance, and I am sure that the wise men of Canada, representing both federal and provincial governments, will not allow constitutional limitations to impede them in formulating the policies that they in their wisdom feel may be necessary.
It is interesting to note, Mr. Chairman, the characteristics we find both in the United

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance
States and to a lesser extent in Canada. This is so because through the wisdom of the Minister of Finance those problems have been anticipated. One sees that the conditions we are faced with in Canada almost meet the classical situation as described by James S. Duesenberry, the cyclical economist, and the great cyclical authority, Dr. Von Haberler. This aspect of economics was studied intensively throughout the 1930's until the outbreak of world war II. In a 1964 publication Dr. Von Haberler gives a description of what we may find in the fourth quarter of the business cycle, and says:
As more and more unemployed factors of production are drawn into employment, the supply of factors of production and of goods in general becomes more and more inelastic, and a constant expansion in terms of money will lead to a smaller and smaller increase in output and to a larger and larger rise in factor and commodity prices. In other words, at the beginning of the expansion, a large part of the increase in monetary circulation will have been absorbed by a rise in the output and turnover of goods, and a smaller part by increasing prices. When full employment is being gradually approached, this necessarily changes.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
Then he went on to say:
When one category of factors after the other is becoming scarce-the transition to full employment is of course gradual and not sudden-it becomes more and more difficult to expand at various points at the same time.
This is the overheating problem, the problem of trying to do too many things at the same time.
If one industry increases its demand for means of production and succeeds in attracting labourers by offering higher wages, it lures them away from other industries. The same holds true of raw materials and semi-finished products. The expansion of the industry is possible only at the expense of a contraction somewhere else.
Mr. Chairman, a Minister of Finance who is not prepared to recognize these things and deal with these matters with the courage and the guts displayed last night has no right, in my way of thinking, to hold this important key office.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Suppose he recognizes these things too late?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: After that investigation I should like to remind hon. members that there was not one pay increase which the official opposition had not pressured.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: We take no responsibility for the two you gave.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: You take no responsibility at all.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
We will take
responsibility when it is ours but we are responsible for nothing like the 30 per cent increase your government approved earlier this year.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: You are mad.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Well, 48 members from the prairies were quite prepared to settle the shipping strike on any terms.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: That was their message to Canada-get the grain moving. This minority government had to survive tests of strength and pressures in this country nearly all of which were challenges to put more money into circulation, even in directions which could not possibly produce more growth.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Everyone in this country is concerned about the situation of the old age pensioners. Members of this house are terribly concerned about those who live on veterans' allowances, about the transport workers-

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Everybody but the pensioners.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: but when there is a condition of virtually full employment, pumping more money into circulation will simply blow the top off.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Exactly what you have done.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
There are some members of the official opposition who do not give a damn about this. Their actions have been neither responsible nor helpful. They do not really care about the overheating process.
Bruce Hutchison asks us whether we have the courage and the wisdom to avoid disaster. The real question before us is not political in the ordinary sense-

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: I rise on a question of privilege. The hon. member has charged that it was the opposition which pumped money into the economy of Canada.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: He did not.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: It is the action taken by the Minister of Finance which has increased the money supply in Canada over the last 18 months.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
The last month.
September 9, 1966

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
The real question is whether we have the courage to do the things which we recognize must be done. As Bruce Hutchison so ably said, the nation itself has been brought to trial.
There are many examples of a more fruitful partnership between labour and management which we could examine. I spent some time in Europe this year and I was much impressed by the co-operation I saw in certain European countries where I found evidence of an increasing understanding in this field which was helpful to all those concerned, to those they loved and to society generally. I commend to the people of Canada the excellent discipline which has been shown by the people of Switzerland where the problems of labour-management relations have been solved for several years, where automation is not opposed and where industry has been so productive and successful that it has been necessary to import workers from abroad to an extent never before equalled.
During the early thirties labour strife had presented such problems that labour and management, which had always considered each other as institutional adversaries-what was good for labour was supposed to be bad for industry, and vice-versa-became fed up with this state of affairs and began to seek a way out of the impasse. Two men, one of them Conrad Ilg, president of the Metalworkers and Watchmakers Union, and the other, Ernest Ducbi, president of the Swiss Association of Industrialists, both of them friends of Albert Schweitzer, were largely responsible for the events which followed. Together they signed a peace agreement for ten years concluding in 1939. This agreement was accepted by all leading unions and it was subsequently extended for three further decades.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member for Leeds but I must remind him that the time allotted for his speech has expired.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Could I be given a few moments more?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Does the hon. member have unanimous consent to continue?

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the matter before us is one of grave national importance-accelerating inflation in respect of which the opposition has asked for action for
Supply-Finance
months and in respect of which the government has failed to act.
Apparently, to judge by the general tenor of speeches made by government members, a new responsibility will rest on members of the opposition-the responsibility for failure to meet the serious situation. Of course, those hon. gentlemen realize that only the government can take action in respect of these matters. Only governments can deal with these things, and members in other parts of the house have neither power nor right to introduce legislation of a financial nature.
We have pressed for action and have been met by derisive contempt. The Minister of Finance has made frightful mistakes. Yesterday he had to admit that he was $150 million out in the estimate he made of expenditure at the time of the introduction of the budget.
We have the cabinet made up of those with orthodox views and also a revisionist group. The Prime Minister belongs to the latter. They make changes from time to time. I can recall no important measure of legislation introduced in this house by the government which has not sooner or later been completely altered. This is a government which does not know where it is going. Over and over again this has been shown. What a galaxy of calisthenic performances we have witnessed with ministers having rugs pulled from under them. It was a performance which the house had never previously seen. Both the Minister of Labour and the Minister of National Health and Welfare made their speeches on the labour question last week, and as they concluded the Prime Minister pulled the rug from under them.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
Again we have an example of another minister in that category, the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Yesterday he found himself in that very uncomfortable position of being flat on the floor because of the action of another minister. What a strange performance between the revisionist and the orthodox groups, the competitors for leadership, a struggle extending far beyond the ordinary purview of the front bench, with each following his own course. I tell the Minister of Finance that recently he was one of the leading horses but he slipped back.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: I still have my smile.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
I do not know what position the Minister of National Health and Welfare now occupies in the race, but from his understandable appearance this morning

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance
it is obvious that he is not pleased. Indeed, last evening when the Minister of Finance spoke on the radio he said in effect, "I can understand he feels badly."
Where is the consistency? The medicare legislation was bruited around as a wonderful piece of work. We said it would not work in the form in which it was presented-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Were you opposed to it?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: -that it could never become effective with some of the provinces not participating. No matter what the government may say, its postponement is simply not on the basis that it would be a contribution to inflation. That is an excuse. It is simply the result of the power struggle going on within the cabinet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Pure fabrication.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
I have heard the minister talk about fabrication previously, and may 1 say there is no one more authoritative on that subject than the hon. gentleman. He does not even know that there is inflation. The copy of his speech that he gave to the press yesterday was headed, "The Need to Prevent Inflation." Doesn't he realize that we are now in the midst of inflation and that it has been accelerating?
I recall when we sat on the government benches and looked at these paragons of political and economic perfection as they told us what to do. I remember what they said: "Place us in office and there will be no more deficits."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: We have reduced them very substantially. We have reduced them down to virtually nothing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: They said, "No more deficits-we have got the solution."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Yes, we use responsibility.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: I realize that the minister is disturbed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
I am not disturbed. I still have
my smile.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
If he is not disturbed then let him just maintain that smiling silence that becomes him so well. They said the day of deficits would be over, and instead of high taxes they were going to cut taxes. In the 1962 and 1963 elections 10,000 scholarships for university students were dangled before the young men and women of the nation. "We will bring them in," said the Prime Minister, "and at once."

Those scholarships were dangled as sugar plums before the eyes of the students of the nation. Now, after three years, the government is going to make a saving by not providing the $10 million for those scholarships. Yet within the last few weeks we have embarked on an extensive expenditure program for other nations, accelerating the expenditures already made by Canada which is contributing greatly to international funds. At the same time the government says to the student body of Canada, "What we promised you we now find, after three and a half years in office, we cannot carry out."
It has been strange to watch this government. It has had recommendations from the Economic Council as to what should be done. It has had the advice of the governor of the Bank of Canada as to what should be done. The minister's speech was headed, "The Need To Prevent Inflation," and there is promise of additional taxes not to meet inflation but to meet other expenditures.
The increases in wages and salaries for the armed forces were announced by Mr. Lee-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Carrots.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
-weeks ago, and he said the amount was going to be large. That is how the government believes it will soften the blow of its ill-digested policies on unification.
Inflation is running wild. They condemned us; but we took measures to get the economy under way. In those days they did not say that the situation in the United States affected Canada, a time when there were 4J million people unemployed in the United States, greater proportionate unemployment than we had, but today they say our difficulties are largely as a result of the situation in the United States. Isn't it strange? But the truth will out.
In the 1962 and 1963 elections they said, "The country is bankrupt." What about the attempted sales of government bonds recently? The reaction of the investing public showed the loss of national confidence in this government.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Now the minister says that the longest period of expansion in the history of the country has taken place, that we have had a long and strong economic expansion in the past five and a half years. That is interesting. They now admit that the expansion began when we were in office, that by our action we started it rolling.
September 9, 1966

Repentance is not always followed by forgiveness. They repent now for the false picture they placed before the people of Canada. They knew better.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: The public won't forgive them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
What about the stock markets? They have gone down and down to the lowest point in two and a half years. What about the interest rates they used to complain about? They are now the highest in 40 years. These things have happened under this government of financial wizards who had all the answers. It is quite a picture. The picture has not been improved by the minister's belated speech yesterday. The night before he spoke on television and gave his considered opinion of the duties of an opposition. He said we were responsible and he could not understand what we were doing.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
I recommend for the minister's reading over the week end the views of the Prime Minister as to the duties of an opposition-I may return to that in detail later-or the views of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that longtime and able parliamentarian who this morning was promoted to the No. 1 position in the leadership stakes of the Liberal party by the Globe and Mail, a position which he will fulfil with dignity. I am referring to his position in the race.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
They say they are a minority government and if they were only a majority government, how they would be able to act. What about their allies? Whenever they need help they are always assured of Social Credit support, no matter what takes place, and this gives them a majority on every occasion. Indeed, the hon. member for Medicine Hat is the waterboy for the Liberal party on almost all occasions. But it is because they are a minority government that they have difficulty and are unable to act, so they say. This represents the attitude of the government but I never expected it to be so clearly revealed as by the minister the night before last when he said:
-this wouldn't matter so much in a house in which we had the dominant majority, but we have slightly fewer than half the members, and therefore what happens in parliament today and the attitude of the opposition is far more important than it has ever been.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
That is right.
Supp ly-Finance

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
When we were in the minority they did not think that. I never heard them arguing that way when we were in the minority. Then there are these immortal words:
If we were sitting there with 175 members we could ignore the opposition-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Read the words.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: This is the verbatim report of the minister's statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Read the words exactly as they are. Read the following sentence.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
The minister said:
If we were sitting there with 175 members we could ignore the opposition and say: "Well, you know that's just what you expect".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Read the next sentence.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Did I not read enough?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: No. Read the next sentence.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
The next sentence is:
But they are sitting in a position of much greater influence upon the outcome and therefore they should have a greater sense of responsibility than they are now exercising.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: The minister has done this before, he is always willing to applaud his own words. This is further evidence of that humility of which we read which is so characteristic of him and is one of his abiding attributes. Is there a national crisis?

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
I think the situation is very, very serious. We have been pointing that out for months. It has been described by the Prime Minister as a disaster. There is fear creeping into the thinking of the people, fear of a potential recession. Have the government acted? They have pushed it aside. The minister does not admit it yet because the heading of his speech is, "The Need To Prevent Inflation".
How is the minister going to prevent inflation? He is going to prevent it by imposing extra taxes so the government will be able to provide for the old age allowance of $105 a month for those in need and extra salary and allowances for the armed forces. Why is there delay in this regard? Inflation has picked the pockets of all Canadians. The depreciating dollar is becoming the vanishing dollar, but the government's attitude, as the heading of the minister's speech says, is still; "The Need To Prevent Inflation".

September 9, 1966
Supp ly-Finance
They said they were going to cut expenditures if they came into office. The minister says: Let us tighten our belts. This government is spending this year $1.6 billion more than we did in the last year we were in office. All across this nation promises were spread around by the Prime Minister-here a building, there a building, here a rink, there a rink. The situation is serious and the responsibility in large measure is the government's.
Somebody suggested today that we were the ones who asked for increased salaries. This government has been piling on high salaries for the top civil servants. Did we ask for those things? What about the expenditures that were expected but now are held up? The dreams of the Minister of National Defence as he marches in martial array into greatness as a competitor in the race? There was to be an expenditure of $100 million for a defence establishment of I do not know how many storeys. They say it will be less than that, but I am referring to the original estimate. Another minister thought we should spend $6 million on a picture. That is the philosophy of the government. Yet the minister tells the people to tighten their belts. Why doesn't he tell that to his colleagues, because they are not doing it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
I have the floor. If the minister wants to answer afterwards, he may. Why doesn't he say that to his colleagues? On every hand they are spending. It has become a colossal race between ministers to find out what new plans they can evolve that will mean the expenditure of money. The government does not yet know that there is inflation, because the subject of the minister's speech was "The Need To Prevent Inflation." Small business across Canada is being driven out on every hand, unable to get money. Interest rates are mounting to a degree never before equalled. What does the government do? It just plays around with this problem. What is the reaction of the small businessman across Canada? Thirty thousand of them in one organization have already asked for guideposts. The Canadian Importers Association has said it has asked for guidelines, as has the Retail Merchants Association. If there be need to establish the fact that there is inflation, you just have to meet the average Canadian today and find out. Last night the minister announced what is described by the Gazette this morning as

the autumn budget. It is a withered leaf. It is
a promise that something is going to be done five, six or seven weeks from now. This government has been very self-satisfied.
[DOT] (1:00 p.m.)
We have been asking for action but we have received only contemptuous and smiling evasions of our requests. Indeed, on July 14 the hon. member for Northumberland asked the government what it was going to do about the situation and the minister said, as recorded at page 7663 of Hansard for that date:
A great deal of our legislation is already having that effect-
He meant that it was containing and counteracting inflation. This government has refused to take any action.
Let me read from a special issue of the Gazette dated September 3, 1966. The heading is "From T-bone Steaks to Cat Food, Prices Are Up, Up...And Up". The article then states:
Across the board, prices on the food market shelves are moving up and up . . . and up.
Sometimes it's only a penny a can, sometimes about 100 per cent increase . . .
The causes are many and varied . . .
Housewives feel the pinch when they pick up a package of bacon priced at $1.35 which sold for 89 cents a year ago and 69 cents the year before that-an impressive and costly increase of almost 100 per cent in two years.
Let me ask this question, and I think the answer is obvious. Who is getting this thick layer of fat?
Let me continue with this article which states:
Tomatoes, which in some stores sold for roughly 15 cents a pound last year, now cost 35 cents a pound in the same stores.
The article then covers the whole picture and states that $10 bought a pile of groceries a year ago but that the same pile of groceries today costs $13.08.
The index does not tell the true story even though it does indicate a tremendous increase. We had the benefit of a speech over the air by the minister in which he suggested that the opposition was to blame, and now we have had the benefit of the speech he made yesterday. We have been asking for action but what is now being produced? What is going to be done to meet the pickpocket of inflation? The President of the United States described inflation in striking phraseology. He said that inflation is an enemy which eventually makes victims of its allies.
September 9, 1966

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: And there is one of the allies speaking now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman holding the powerful position of Minister of Finance says that we are the allies of inflation. Is it any wonder that one begins to question his thinking regarding the function of an opposition? What he says is that if we were not here in large opposition the government could tell us to take a jump in the lake. That is his attitude and it is a denial of the basic principles of democracy and parliamentary government. The minister knows that, but he still has that senior civil service mentality that affects so many of the frontbenchers of the Liberal party.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has never learned anything.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Prices are increasing at a gallop but we find that farmers are not reaping the benefits of these tremendous increases. I do not have the latest figures available but as of 1965 the farmers' share of the dollar paid by consumers was 40 cents generally across the board.
The government is going to increase taxes. It increased taxes last April by 10 per cent to be paid by all except about 40 per cent of the people. What effect did that have? It now takes about 14 hours of a 40-hour week for the average Canadian taxpayer to pay for federal, provincial and municipal taxes. Prices are increasing as never before and the minister says that some action should be taken to meet potential inflation. His words, undertakings and actions are almost effective as a rubber mallet. He tells the people not to spend too much and to start saving something. Perhaps the government should think of doing the same. The government suggests that action must be taken, but the action they recommend is nothing more than a palliative caricature of action.
What will be the result of the announcement made by the minister that within a month or six weeks there is going to be a baby budget? He has announced in advance what it is going to contain. This is the first time I have ever known such an unconstitutional thing to happen, at least since Mr. Gordon had three boys fix up his budget. The minister announced that there would be action five, six or seven weeks from now. I can now only think that the hon. member for Davenport, the former minister of finance, will become even more attractive to his supporters 23033-523
Supply-Finance
than he has been, at least by comparison, because what he did appears to be brilliant compared to what this minister has done in announcing what action will be taken six weeks from now.
What will be the effect of this announcement? What will the individual do as a result of the knowledge that something is going to be done? Business will be unable to make plans, not knowing exactly what is going to happen. Everyone will want to know when, how and where tax increases will hit. I suggest that the minister's announcement will bring about the greatest uncertainty in the economic field that this country has ever known. Everyone will have to look ahead weeks before knowing what they should do.
I do not think the government has any plans. They have not been able to bring together the orthodox and the revisionists with the result that they have no plans. They now suggest that if we get out of here they will go to work and come up with something. We want action to be taken and we want it to be taken now, not next month. We are here now and we should deal with the situation. The question of inflation is the most important matter facing Canada today. What will happen in the next six weeks? Prices will climb and climb and individuals will hoard and accumulate. The result will be economic uncertainty in the nation. Why not bring in legislation now? That is a very simple question.
Our attitude is this. Canada faces a difficult situation and unpopular courses must be followed. If the government will go ahead and act now instead of playing with this problem, we will co-operate to the fullest degree in taking effective action in the national interest. [DOT] (1:10 p.m.)
The minister has not as yet put forward one suggestion of any effective action to be taken. By how much is he going to cut expenditures of various departments today accelerating? Why is it that in his estimate of expenditures he is already out by $150 million since the budget was brought in? Can something not be done to control these grasping ministers, each building an empire for himself?
We want action now. If the minister will propose effective action we will be prepared to stay and support it to the fullest degree. As a result of his failure to act, we are faced with a national crisis. We will co-operate by supporting effective legislation. We ask the minister to take action rather than tell us to go home now and deal with the Bank Act

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance
when we come back. How they kicked the matter around to find an interest rate, and what fighting went on in the cabinet between the orthodox and the revisionists. The fight is still on.
While they disagree the economy suffers. They proclaim in loud voices what they will do five or six weeks from now and they swallow silently when action should be taken now. Why not bring in legislation? What intermediate measures has the minister in mind? Let him bring them in. Postponing action for weeks will result in employees stiffening their demands. What about the small group which profiteers at the expense of the nation? What will they do during that five or six-weeks period? They will be encouraged. About two months will elapse before legislation can be brought in. They will be two months of grace extended to the hoarders and to those who will make a run on durable goods. An upward pressure of prices will result. There can be consumer panic in the face of threatened legislation if action is not taken immediately. We ask for that action.
In the field of labour the government, by the 30 per cent settlement which was brought about in Montreal and on the Great Lakes, made it impossible for the responsible union leaders of this country to stand. The Pearson formula is now accepted as having received governmental approval. We were not to blame for that, were we? We asked you to get it settled.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: That is right, at any price.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: That there was a suggestion that the matter be settled at any price is an unadulterated departure from the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Just as is what the hon. gentleman has now said.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
I do not think that what I just said was unparliamentary. If it was, I will substitute for it by saying that this is another of the minister's terminological inexactitudes.
Why did you not bring the matter of the 30 per cent settlement before the house? You wanted to play around with the problem and bring about a solution by offering more than was actually asked for in one case, I believe, so that you would be known for settling labour difficulties. You set greater fires of inflation than have ever existed before. What is happening? Profits of food companies are going up and up. A committee will be set up
[Mr. Diefenbaker.!
by the house to ascertain what is happening. What has the government been doing? While pockets were being picked by inflation the guardian and his government were asleep. I say this in spite of the highly commendatory eulogy of the minister given by the hon. gentleman who preceded me. He deserves a promotion.
What about prices of commodities in the future? I quote a man who is politically removed and therefore cannot be suspected of being activated by other than the facts of life. He is Maurice Amyot, president of the Grocers' Association of the province of Quebec. The day before yesterday, September 7 Le Soleil quoted him as saying: "Prices for groceries are going up 15 per cent to 18 per cent in 1967." These are the facts and the government will not act. Surely the minister should decide that the time has come to act now. Last March he gave a clarion call for restraint, but it fell on deaf ears. The deafest ears were those of his cabinet colleagues.
This government does not follow its own rules. The newspapers reported the Minister of Industry as saying that Canada had bought seven jets from France which would be used by cabinet ministers.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to repeat that misrepresentation. The statement has been denied categorically a dozen times.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: It has been denied but the purchase has not. It was a completely unnecessary and unjustifiable expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that the transport services of the department are unnecessary.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
The government does not wish to bear the expenditure which they ask other people to bear but they willingly impose taxes.
What action can the minister take at this time? I would think that, having regard for the constitutional position and in co-operation with the provinces, he should endeavour to bring about agreement for legislation to be passed by both the federal parliament and the provinces. Indeed, when I suggested it the Prime Minister admitted that this was going to be done. On August 29 I asked that the government call together the provinces with a view to reaching an agreement on some form of co-operative legislation. The reply of
September 9, 1966

the Prime Minister, as it appears in Hansard of that day at page 7761, was:
Mr. Speaker, on September 14 there is to be a meeting between the federal and provincial ministers of finance. This very important matter is on the agenda and will be discussed with the provincial ministers of finance at that time.
[DOT] (1:20 p.m.)
When the provincial treasurers across this nation heard about it they said: "There is nothing to it, we have never heard about it." The Minister of Finance answered for the Prime Minister two days later and said that there should be action along that line. The provinces are just as anxious as we in the federal arena that galloping inflation shall be met. The Premier of Quebec announced yesterday he is going to set up a committee of the legislature to consider this matter.
There should be a strengthening of the combines investigation staff so that a thorough examination may be made into unjust price fixing, price fixing resulting from demand. There should be set up immediately a price spreads commission. The information is largely available now through the Economic Council. In addition, there should be the fullest investigation into the whole problem of unjust and unfair profiteering. It is occurring. All you have to do is go to the stores and markets to know that today's price is different tomorrow. Yet we are asked at this time and under these circumstances to wait another five, six or seven weeks so the government can think of some plan.
So serious is the matter in connection with food that if one examines the periodicals one finds that in many cases food items are 25 per cent higher than in the United States. Why is this so? We want action. We are prepared to stay here. Produce your legislation. Do not postpone consideration for six weeks. At the rate prices are going up the dollar will be a vanishing dollar. The problem is a tremendous one. The implications to our nation demand action. The suggestion was made by the hon. gentleman who preceded me that, whatever the constitutional difficulties, we do not have to pay attention to them; at least, that is how I interpreted his words. I do not accept that view. I believe that the provinces would be only too willing to co-operate to meet a problem that is eating at the vitals of this nation.
No longer can the minister say that the opposition is to blame. Bring in your legislation. You have always tried to tie somebody to the stake for your responsibility. As I listened to the minister the other night I must
23033-523J
Supply-Finance
say that his description of me, by inference, could only be applied to His Satanic Majesty. I am to blame for almost everything. No matter what this government does not do, it is the Leader of the Opposition who is to blame. When I think of the three or four years of calumny that has been heaped on me, when I think of the colouring books, the truth squads, the pigeons, and all those other instruments, mental offspring of some of the members now sitting on the front bench, I realize that they have tried everything. Those in the press who support them have joined in. They pictured me as suffering from an incurable disease. I have an incurable disease and it is this, the desire to do something for Canada.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
They spread these falsehoods. They put them in their literature. However, I never expected that a man with the wide experience and benevolent appearance of the Minister of Finance would go on television and place the responsibility on the opposition. We say to you now that many of the things you have done we pressed for. You did not want to do them but you had to do them for the benefit of the people. We say to you now, keep parliament going. Do not send us home. Act now, because what you have done in the production or revelation of a budget to be introduced only in six or seven weeks is a constitutional contravention. It is a detriment to Canada. We ask you to bring in your baby budget now. Certainly, it did not take long for the gestation. One day the government said it was not going to have it and the next day the government said, we are going to produce a baby budget. Bring it in and we will join with you in a spirit of co-operation in the national interest provided you do something effective, because this is a dangerous situation.
I am not very hopeful that the challenge will be accepted because you have not an idea in the world about what should be done under the circumstances except to criticize the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Would the right hon. gentleman permit just one question, Mr. Chairman, a very mild one? Is it not so that you give notice of budgets quite a long way in advance? This has been our constitutional practice for years and years and was the practice of the right hon. gentleman.

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Always, but you have already said what you are going to do. You have said, we are going to have a budget but this time you have said what you are going to have in the budget, including taxation in order to cover certain matters. This is where you made your mistake.
