speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: I deny this categorically and I defy the right hon. gentleman to show any-were in the statement I made anything of that nature except with respect to one matter already announced to this house, namely, that when the guaranteed income program was brought forward there would be an increase in taxes. This is well known. Otherwise I was very careful to make it clear I was not committed to do anything else.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Not committed to do anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Exactly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: I agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Have it whichever way you want.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: The last word of the minister was, "exactly", and Hansard has it.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, yesterday morning a social worker called me from Vancouver. She was deeply concerned about the impending debate on inflation and the cost of living, and she communicated with me to find out whether anything was known or could be gathered about what was going to be done. She was concerned not only about the low income groups but because of the general state of affairs in the city of Vancouver where the cost of living is now beginning to cut deeply into the moderate income groups above the poverty level with which social workers are concerned. I was not, of course, able to tell her anything about what would be in the minister's statement. However, I know quite well how that social worker is feeling today. I believe that even in her deepest moments of concern she could not have foreseen the completely devastating statement made by the Minister of Finance last evening.
[DOT] (1:30 p.m.)
I do not want to misquote the Minister of Finance so I will use his exact words as they appear in Hansard. First of all, in regard to the winter housebuilding program he said

that the decision had been taken to discontinue the winter housebuilding incentive program. In regard to research grants he said that the government will have to exercise more restraint in the rate of increase this year. The minister may explain that in any way he sees fit, but to the ordinary person that means in plain English a cut-back in research grants.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Yes, that is what it means in plain English.
Then the Minister of Finance went on to say that the scholarship program, which it had been the original intention of the government to introduce this year, will be deferred, but he made no attempt to say for how long.
Fourth, he said that the agreements with the provinces in support of certain forestry programs expire next March and the government has decided that they should not be renewed because, he added, the government felt that the provinces could carry on without such programs. That is again a highly debatable point, especially if the views of the provinces are taken into consideration.
In regard to medicare I would not even try to paraphrase what he said but will read his words from Hansard as they are recorded on page 8217:
We have decided that we must defer the commencement of one major program that is already before the house. Many of the provincial governments have indicated that they feel we are attributing too much urgency to the introduction of full medicare programs right away, and they do not feel prepared to proceed to put such programs into effect next summer as provided for in the bill before the house. We therefore propose to defer the effective date of the plan for a year until July 1, 1968. The legislation will be proceeded with in the house as a high priority item when we reassemble at the beginning of October. The government has no intention of changing the substance of the bill other than its effective date.
I wanted to say "dishonest" but I do not know whether that expression is parliamentary. In any event, it is not honest to say that this matter has high priority and should be rushed through the house this fall when it is pigeonholed until one year from now. No one in this country will be fooled by such tactics. People know that this is merely a device to try to trap the public into thinking that the matter is being advanced a stage further.
Let me suggest, Mr. Chairman, that what the minister did last night in this regard was to put the whole medicare scheme back a long, long way. We were on the verge of
September 9, 1966

having that scheme in June had we given first reading to the bill that afternoon. Now neither the government nor anybody else knows when medicare will become effective, its date of application. What some of us said in June is equally true now, namely, that the interval of time between today and July 1, 1968 is going to be used by all of the forces opposed to medicare in order to delay and, if possible, prevent entirely the bringing in of a medicare scheme.
In regard to old age pensions, let me again repeat the words of the minister relating to that other big program, as reported at page 8217 of Hansard:
When we have before us, perhaps in late October, the measures to authorize the increased revenues made necessary by the income guarantee plan we will be able to review our general fiscal position and consider what changes are desirable in the light of the economic and financial situation.
Translated into plain English, this means that the whole question of an increase for the old age pensioners is once again left in doubt. Perhaps the Minister of Finance knows when the matter will again be brought forward, but outside of the Minister of Finance nobody has any idea when in the world anything will be done for the old age pensioners of this country. This is true also of members of the government. I suggest that what this debate and the announcement of the Minister of Finance yesterday have done is to reveal beyond the shadow of a doubt who is the strong man in the Liberal government. There may have been doubts about it before but I do not think there remains even a shadow of a doubt now.
The Minister of Labour got his some time ago, as did the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Manpower. Each one of them was slapped down, and we now finally see who is the real boss in the cabinet, the Minister of Finance. He has shown that the reason he is boss is that he speaks for the people for whom this government is really legislating, the big financial and corporate interests of Canada. This has been revealed by this debate. That is how we feel about it.
Yet, Mr. Chairman, this is the government that less than a year ago went on platforms throughout the country and on the radio and television stations of Canada and said to the people of the country: "Elect us and we will give you a winter works program and other necessary things which should be done. We will give you a vastly increased research program. We will give you programs to aid
Supply-Finance
the students in our universities and other institutions of higher learning. We will give you a medicare program absolutely, definitely and unshakably, by July 1, 1967. We will give you a better deal for the old age pensioners". The Prime Minister was reported to have said that the better deal would be in the neighbourhood of $125 a month.
These are the things which were said by this government when they were purporting to represent all of the people of this country. They made a particular appeal to the people who really wanted help from government, people with low incomes, people who were less secure and had less of the affluent society which we are told exists around us. All this has happened this year.
I contend that the people of Canada are not going to be deceived now by these lame excuses. The government has shown whom it is really representing. It is the big, vested financial and corporate interests of this country. I do not care what the members of the government say. Let them wag their heads in denial. When the chips are down and the programs come in, these are the people who benefit from the fiscal and economic policies which are being put forward by the government. This was demonstrated only too well and too thoroughly by the Minister of Finance yesterday.
The former minister of agriculture referred to the statement of the Minister of Finance yesterday as being a complete victory for the establishment. I call it a devastating defeat for the ordinary people of this country. Still further, I call it a "punish the poor" policy. We have always known that the worst crime to commit in this country is to be poor. We now find that the punishment is fitting the crime and becoming the most severe punishment imaginable, a cutting off of the very means which are needed in order to have a moderate and decent sort of living standard in this country.
I want to indicate, as I have already said, that those who get hurt the most by these policies are those who are the least able to protect themselves. A number of us have been brought up to admire the tradition of the sea, which is something we in this western democracy should be proud of. In cases of shipwreck or disasters at sea the tradition is for women and children, the weak and helpless, to go to the lifeboats first while the others, the strong men, stay on deck and go down with the ship if there are insufficient safety devices available for all.

September 9, 1966
Supp ly-Finance
What do we find in the statement of the minister, Mr. Chairman? At the first sign of economic heavy weather the women and children, the sick and the poor, the helpless and the young people who need education, are herded not into the lifeboats but are dumped into the sea so that there will be easier going for those whom this government is really seeking to protect. Let us not fool ourselves about that. That sort of thing is not going to stop with low income groups.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)
I well remember a story that hon. members will have read in their school days. I refer to the Masque of the Red Death by Edgar Allan Poe. In the story the powerful, the affluent and the comfortable seated themselves in a castle while the red death was raging outside, under the impression that they were secure because they were comfortable and because their incomes were sufficient, so to speak. They thought they were protected from the read death outside. As the story goes on, a horrible certitude creeps in that the red death in time will penetrate even to these people in the very centre of comfort and security. This is what will happen if we continue with this sort of policy, because what is wrong with the Canadian economy is that it suffers from a complete maldistribution of income, power and wealth. This is what must be dealt with.
I will read the testimony of a couple of witnesses. Here is what Claude Jodoin, President of the Canadian Labour Congress, said recently:
Worry about inflation never seems to arise until workers ask for their share of an even more prosperous economy. Wage increases obtained by some groups this year have followed huge rises in corporation profits and an increase in the cost of living. Looking at the Canadian economic scene as a whole, we find that between 1961 and 1965 corporation profits, after taxes, rose by 67 per cent while, in the same period, average weekly wages and salaries went up only 16 per cent. It is obvious that Canadian corporations have not only failed to share this prosperity with their employees but they have also deprived Canadian consumers of benefits which could have been provided by these prosperous conditions.
If we had a government that was concerned about protecting the people of this country and the consumers of this country, surely it would be proposing that corporations, the profits of which have risen by 67 per cent, should be heavily taxed rather than blaming the poor or groups such as railway workers who have demanded increased wages so that they can have enough to live on. This is the sort of thing I am talking about.
[Mrs. Maclnnis (Vancouver-Kingsway).l
I shall now quote another witness. He is a former vice president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Before that he was the president of the Farmers Union in Alberta. This is what he had to say the other day:
In the past 15 to 20 years, the dollar return to the farmer for farm produce has been, on the average, less than the take-home pay of labourers working for $1.00 per hour or less. Within the total group of farmers are some 10 per cent who, because of certain circumstances or conditions, are able to maximize these returns into large incomes.
Another 20 per cent manage fairly well and depend on inflated land values to give them a decent retirement fund. The other 70 per cent continue on a day to day basis with day to day commitments that are dependent on their ability to sell something even if that sale gives them no profit. Their whole situation is created because of their effort to get into the 30 per cent category by operating on term credit.
And so on. This farmer is not taken in by the language that has been used about labour to the effect that it is the organized trade unions that are robbing him of the value of his produce. He puts the matter better than I could and I will use his words. He says:
The real issue is the continuation of archaic attitude toward the distribution of wealth and purchasing power. It is the attitude that some people have more right to wealth than others. It is the attitude that some people make greater contributions to the production of wealth than do others. It is the attitude that insists the only way that wealth should be distributed is by the individual's capacity to compete for it, without recognizing the fact that there is no longer any free competition between individuals for the wealth they, as a whole or a group, make available to a nation.
It is imperative therefore that at this particular time it is necessary to rise above the side issues presently being argued in the press, radio and street corners. The rail strike, packinghouse strike and various other protest actions are only symptoms of the real crisis, maldistribution of purchasing power.
These are the things that we agree with. We say at this time, when we speak of inflation and other economic difficulties, that to use the present policies against the poor, against those of modest income, against the farmers, the organized workers and the sick, is merely compounding the difficulties and setting aside terrible troubles for a day of reckoning that is bound to come.
We must stop talking in terms of averages. The trouble is that we think of people in great big lumps. We have come to the conclusion that because the average person is getting along all right and the average wage or average income is adequate, we need not worry. That was exactly what was said by the smiling face of the Minister of Finance as he assured us that everything was just fine. God is in his heaven, everything is all right
September 9, 19G6

in his world. But the Liberal party is not managing to deceive the rest of us about what is going on in the country.
It is not true that people are averages. Averages do not eat, wear clothes, pay rent. But people do need food and do pay rent and wear clothing. We must provide ways and means for people to be able to do these things.
We must stop using the old cliches. We must stop kidding ourselves with cliches and get down to the business of finding out how to provide a decent, reasonable standard of living for the people of this country. There are people in this house who have been impressed with the elaborate economic jargon we have heard. I say to them that there are many people in Canada who believe that the business of government is to run the affairs of the country so that every man, woman and child in the country will have a chance to have a modern, decent standard of living. It is the business of government to provide a contribution to the welfare of the country to make that standard of living possible. That is what we are here to do.
We have to do two things. First, we must establish a guaranteed annual income for the people of Canada. We have got to do that today, without waiting for this year, next year, some time or never. As I say, we must do that now. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has been talking to people about the need of having a guaranteed annual income. The Liberals of western Canada, when they met recently, passed a resolution urging that the question of a guaranteed annual income be gone into. The Minister of Agriculture has provided some sort of guaranteed income for farmers who give up their farms under the ARDA program. That has been embodied in the agreement between the federal government and the province of Ontario.
In a recent editorial the Vancouver Sun, which is as staunch a Liberal party organ as can be found in this country, had this to say on August 1 of this year:
The idea of a national guaranteed income is worth considering. Credit must go to Health Minister Allan MacEachen for raising the possibility during his recent visit to Vancouver.
And so on. Then, going on to examine certain things that have been raised in the Liberal party, it says:
There are, however, a lot of questions to be posed. Can you guarantee an income and a cost of living to match it? Is it right to propose a costly
Supply-Finance
welfare program in times of inflation? Most important, would GI destroy incentive?
There is raised the curious possibility that in a Utopian society circa 2,000 we might work for fun because we'd all be paid a fixed wage for doing nothing.
But it could well be that a guaranteed income is the most effective method of fighting poverty, ensuring employment, promoting stability in labour-management relations and administering welfare.
It can be done without the kind of means test which is so abhorrent to critics of the present welfare system, either by straight subsidy or by a negative income tax.
It is worth a look; but a very sober and far-seeing look.
That is not a sudden convert to socialism speaking, or anything like that. That is the very sober and sometimes very reactionary Vancouver Sun editorially speaking words of sense and of good, sound wisdom in this instance.
[DOT] (1:50 p.m.)
I suggest that if the Minister of Finance would try to find ways and means of putting buying power into the hands of the poor, those who need it, many difficulties would be solved and there would be no need to pace the boom and so on. He should do some solid thinking about getting a guaranteed income into the hands of the public because it has been seen that a guaranteed income works very well for some of us. The minister should pay some heed to the case for getting a guaranteed income into the hands of the people who need it today. Guaranteed income works beautifully for members of parliament. It works beautifully for senators. It works beautifully for civil servants. Why would it not work well for people who have no means of getting a good steady income or enough income to make a decent standard of living possible? This is one of the things that should be done right now to deal with the situation.
A second is to explore ways and means of stabilizing the cost of 1'iving at a level which those on guaranteed incomes can afford to pay. The two are tied inextricably together and cannot be dealt with separately.
I know the Minister of Finance will be attending a conference with the premiers of the provinces in the coming week. I also know, because he has told us so, that he is not going there with any plan having to do with prices and wages. I wish that for once this federal government would go to such a conference with a program to lay before the premiers.
I agree entirely with the views of the Leader of the Opposition on this point. I

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance
believe the provinces would welcome a well-conceived plan from the federal government designed to stabilize the cost of living for the consumers of this country at least as far as food, clothing, rent, household articles and medical care are concerned. These are things about which the provinces are worried and there is no reason in the world why the Minister of Finance should not go to this conference to seek a delegation of provincial powers to the federal government in order to help stabilize the cost of living and fight inflation. Certainly it would be a brave provincial government which would say no if the federal government had a good plan for stabilizing the cost of living and if it sought a delegation of provincial powers to enable it to carry out at least the beginnings of such a plan. I believe this should be done.
There are, of course, many difficulties in the way. The minister has spoken about difficulties. He should know what they are because he had a hand in this sort of thing as a civil servant during the second world war. I suggest that the real difficulties are neither constitutional nor administrative. What really prevents the Prime Minister going to the provinces with a program to stabilize the cost of living is the absence of the will to do it. That is the greatest difficulty. The Minister of Finance and the cabinet behind him have today proven that they are the servants not of the people of Canada who need them but of the people who do not need them, the big financial concerns and corporations of this country who can help themselves and who have already done so.
I wish to turn to some of the things which we believe should be done and deal with them briefly. We believe a start should be made by reversing the decision to cut back certain programs. Provision for medicare and the old age security program should be continued as formerly planned. To cut these things is a disaster. The old age pensioners have scarcely been able to wait until the fall in order to get some relief. How will they greet the news that the government intends when the fall comes only to look at the fiscal situation and see whether anything should be done?
We believe the Prime Minister should go to the provincial conference with a plan to stabilize the cost of living. Parliament has already shown that it can and will place curbs on wages. It has done so. I suggest there are thousands and thousands of people in this country who will not be afraid of measures to

control the prices of the things they need in order to enjoy a decent living standard. The only people who are afraid are the people who stand to lose by such a program of stabilization and control.
I think it is a good idea to get an investigation of this whole subject under way but I am under no illusion that this is likely to be a fast-acting procedure. I would point out that in the United States they have gone ahead a great deal faster than we have in Canada along these lines. On August 3 the Senate agriculture committee asked Secretary of Agriculture Orville L. Freeman to investigate recent increases in prices for milk, bread and other foodstuffs throughout the country. He got busy right away and asked the federal trade commission to investigate. In the course of its inquiries, which have been under way for most of the month of August, the commission brought to light some interesting facts which I should like to draw to the attention of the government.
Mr. Freeman himself testified before the city council committee in Manhattan. There and elsewhere he absolved the farmer from blame for escalating prices. He declared that while farm prices rose 6 per cent in the past year they are still nearly 2 per cent below the base period of 1947-1949, though retail food prices are 34 per cent higher.
Further, he declared that in 1965 consumers paid a total of $77.6 billion for farm-produced food, up $34 billion from the base period. Of this gain he said that only $6.6 billion, or 19.3 per cent, "trickled down to the farmer". At the same hearing representative Lester Wolff, Democrat, New York, a former marketing consultant, laid the blame for some of the spiraling prices of bread and milk on wasteful delivery methods and collusive and corrupt practices.
At the same hearing officials of the Farmers Union and other farm groups argued that the farmer cannot be blamed for the price hikes in bread or other products. One of them, Harry L. Graham, cited a pattern of monopolistic price fixing and organization in the bakery field. In the meantime, representative Leonard Farbstein introduced a bill to impose a 90-day freeze on food prices. This was needed, he argued, in order to halt inflation.
These are some of the things that are going on in the United States. They are getting along much faster there than we are in Canada. Reference was made yesterday by my hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands to sacred cows. In Canada profits
September 9, 1966

have always been regarded as sacred cows not to be touched. But these things are changing. I read the other day that in India they are beginning to look around for ways and means of controlling the population of sacred cows in that country. They have even been suggesting that birth control might well be tried out on sacred cows as a means of popularizing it in other quarters.
I know these things will not be easy. But I also know they can be done by a government which really wants to do them. They have been done in time of war. The period in which we are now living may be a period of prosperity for a few people but it is a period of depression and misery for a great many. The alternative to action is strikes and more strikes as the stronger and better organized workers try to protect themselves, leaving those who are less well organized in still greater misery while those on the land are forced to abandon their job of food production.
[DOT] (2:00 p.m.)
Increasing numbers of people will be forced on to the relief rolls because they are not getting enough money to live on and the stage will be set for chaos and disorder. I suggest that now, before we are confronted with run-away inflation, is the time to deal with these things. I suggest that now, before inflation gets carried away by its own momentum, we should deal with it.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it can be seen from the speech made by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), notwithstanding the opinion of the hon. members sitting opposite, that logical measures will be applied to remove the spectre of inflation.
Any objective measure in the interest of the Canadian people makes sense. We must admit that certain signs show that the danger of inflation exists. Canadians are going through a period of prosperity at the present time, a period of sound and productive investments. The economic growth we are experiencing is rational and supported by a tendency to consume more than we can produce. It is therefore useless to repeat here the percentages concerning manpower and productivity already mentioned.
Although in some areas of our production, consumption and productivity are balanced, in other areas a little more time will be needed before this equilibrium is reached by
Supply-Finance
filling the gaps in manpower. One may gather upon hearing the speech made by the hon. Minister of Finance that the harsh measures mentioned in his speech, are timely throughout Canada. The cost of labour and social welfare programs, in relation to demand, is excessive; every citizen is partly responsible for the increase in prices. Under such circumstances, how can a responsible government act? As the minister has so rightly stated, and as several editorial writers have been repeating in the morning papers, it is by taking restrictive measures. For instance, by controlling capital expenditures, while giving priority to certain programs which are particularly stimulating for our national economy and maintaining full employment. Some social welfare measures will be deferred. Obviously, this is unacceptable to a party, from a political point of view, but you will agree that, in order to face up to such a situation, the government has no other alternative.
I see nothing drastic about the discipline which all Canadians should impose upon themselves. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) repeated this during the last election campaign. We have seen several countries, which may not have experienced a situation similar to ours, accept to tighten their belt. New taxes may be levied, and provincial programs may also be viewed with a critical eye.
The situation in which we find ourselves today is being reflected tenfold. As for the social measures mentioned in the statement of the Minister of Finance, the poorer people of the country would be affected. Every measure included in this consolidation program will be applied, possibly at a later date, and they may also turn against the Minister of Finance and possibly the government.
Everything has been put aside to prove once again that leadership is a characteristic of the Liberal party.
Our country has progressive economists and other objectives; all that is needed is to weigh the welfare of all Canadians in all areas of our economy. Our financial and banking system is the best organized in the world, in spite of what some opposition party may claim; our institutions play an all-important role and, in years gone by, they have been a stepping-stone for our economy. These institutions have supplied statistics and surveys and have helped the government to complement controls without the least restrictive effects, which could have slowed down

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance
the implementation of theories concerning productivity, manpower and consumption.
Industry alone controls our future as long as its development remains under Canadian control.
Enough pomposity; let us see action. I believe the program announced by the Minister of Finance must provide the assurance that we will go through this crisis and come out stronger than before.
We must understand that we are part of an economic entity very closely related to our neighbour to the south.
Mr. Chairman, let us ignore the gibes of the opposition, their empty speeches, their destructive criticisms, and let us show that we are the government, and let us govern in the best interest of all Canadians.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when he gave his presentation yesterday the Minister of Finance simply described the situation which everyone in Canada knows very well exists in this country today. He told us nothing new, and he merely announced several additional negative steps which the government intends to take to try to shore up its obvious failure to curb inflation. During his presentation the minister very nearly broke his wrist trying to pat himself and the government on the back for what he termed the excellent job which the government had done in controlling inflation. I suggest it might be profitable for us to look at just what the government has done in this matter since the minister presented his budget last spring.
In his budget the minister forecast that during the next 12 months there would be an increase in the price level of between 3J and 4 per cent. According to Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures released yesterday, the price index during the past 12 months has risen 5.5 per cent, and at this very moment is increasing at the rate of 7.2 per cent for a whole year.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
This increase will go up even faster in the months ahead because of the 30 per cent wage increase guide lines which the government established a few months ago. The reason is, and it is obvious, that no union leader will dare to propose to his members that they accept anything less than a 30 per cent increase in wages because he knows that if he does he will be looking for a new job in the very near future. His union members will simply say to him, "The union leader of the

Montreal dock workers got his people 30 per cent. The union leader of the seaway workers got his people 30 per cent, and these were authorized by the government of Canada. If you cannot get us 30 per cent then we will get somebody who can." That is the reason no union leader can agree on behalf of his members to accept anything less than a 30 per cent wage increase in the future.
Let there be no doubt that when the negotiations between the railway workers and railway management are concluded some time this autumn, the wage increase will amount to at least 30 per cent. These 30 per cent settlements, the pattern of which was set by the government last spring, will of course be passed on to the consumer, and will by that amount accelerate the rise in the cost of living.
If the program for controlling inflation which the government have been following is considered by them to be a success-and according to the minister's statement yesterday he obviously considers it is a success-I should like the minister to explain to the house what his idea of a failure would be. As I have said, the increase in the cost of living has been accelerating almost day by day. Several months ago the minister forecast an increase of 3J per cent to 4 per cent. Yesterday it was announced by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics that the increase between August of last year and August of this year was, 5.5 per cent. During July the increase was 7.2 per cent, calculated on a yearly basis.
The causes of these increases are happening almost hourly. I learned during the lunch interval that the Minister of Agriculture, in a conference which he held this morning and at a press conference which he gave afterwards to announce the results, said that the cost of butter to the consumer was to be increased by 2 cents a pound and he promised consideration of an increase in the price of other products to the consumer. So we see that daily, almost hourly, this government, by increasing prices to the consumer, by entering into wage negotiations and forcing their views upon those negotiations, is increasing the cost of living by its direct action.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, there is no question that the problem of inflation lies squarely on the shoulders of this government, and it is absolutely ridiculous for members of the government to claim that the opposition is irresponsible in this regard. I have already since the first of the year made several speeches in this house pointing out to the
September 9, 1966

government what would happen if they continued to maintain their present policies. I pointed out the inflation that would take place, and the results that would accrue from that inflation. My colleagues, to mention only two, from Prince Edward-Lennox and Simcoe East last spring also made very effective speeches, and almost every member of this party has been making presentations to the house outlining to the government what was going on from their personal experience regarding the increase in the cost of living.
We have been making positive suggestions as to what could and should be done to control the increase in the cost of living but we have always been ignored. We have been told that the government was pursuing the best of all possible plans, that the country had nothing to worry about, and all we had to do was sit tight, say nothing and put our faith in the government. The figures I have mentioned today outline clearly that we have come to a very serious state of affairs in this country and that from now on the voice of the opposition must be heeded by this government, because obviously they are unable to discern themselves what is the problem, what should be done about it, and present to the house concrete plans for dealing with it.
It is obvious to all of us that we are in a crisis situation regarding this runaway inflation, and that is not too strong a word to apply to it. It must be controlled. But unfortunately the government's plans, as they were announced by the Minister of Finance in his budget last spring and in his presentation to the house yesterday, are both negative and sterile. They are out of date. They are the old plans that were used many, many years ago and it is about time this country was treated to something more imaginative, something more modern and something more effective.
A good example of this sterile and negative attitude was illustrated in the minister's speech yesterday when he announced that the government intended to slow down the assistance which is being given to research and defer their scholarship program. As we know, one of the chief causes of inflation is low productivity which sends costs and prices up. Two of the best ways to increase productivity are, first, to increase research and, second, to increase scientific education. Through both these methods we will find out what are the best products for us to produce and better methods to produce those products. By adopting these methods we can increase productivity, lower costs, thereby lower selling prices and thus control inflation.
23033-524J
Supply-Finance
But what do we find this government doing? They are cutting out or greatly diminishing their assistance to two of the programs that can assist this country in fighting inflation. The kind of sterile, negative program which this government is following will achieve the same results as did an exactly similar program in late 1956 and early 1957, when their tight money policy and negative approach brought on a recession which was well launched when the Conservative party took office on June 21 of that year.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I think we should examine this question and see what can be done to deal with the problem of inflation in a positive rather than negative manner. We know that inflationary pressures are caused by too much money chasing too few goods. We know that these pressures can be reduced either by the negative method of decreasing the volume of money available to chase the goods or by the positive method of increasing the volume of goods available for purchase.
As one would expect, knowing this government, they chose the negative method and have been reducing the volume of money steadily over the past year by doing two things, first, increasing taxes and, second, imposing a tight money policy on the economy of this country. A young and growing country with Canada's potential for growth should be increasing, not decreasing, production, and it is shameful that we should be adopting the negative policy of decreasing production at this time. Increasing production was the policy of the Conservative party when we formed the government from 1957 to 1963, and that will be our policy when we form a government again in the very near future.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
We have a right to ask ourselves why this government is not following such a positive program. The answer is that this situation resulted from a critical shortage of skilled labour in this country which this government permitted to occur. During the past year this shortage has become more and more evident. For some time it has been clear that the technical training schools which were established when we were in government and which have been doing a good job are unable to produce a sufficient number of skilled workers each year to allow production to expand fast enough to meet the demand for products both here in Canada and in export markets.
Supply-Finance

September 9, 1966
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
Earlier this year I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce why our exports were not increasing at a faster rate and he replied that we in Canada could not produce enough goods to satisfy the Canadian demand and a growing world market demand. That is a shocking admission for the government to make. Once world markets are lost and customers find alternative sources of supply they are very often reluctant to return to the original sources. We are losing sales abroad which we will probably never recapture and we are losing the sales because we cannot produce enough in this country to meet the demand.
As a result of the shortage of skilled workers we do not produce enough goods to satisfy the expanding potential world markets or the Canadian demand which has grown tremendously because Canada has become an affluent society. This situation has caused inflation which is the problem with which we are faced today. Because Canada is an affluent society there is a great deal of money available for the purchase of consumer goods. People wish to satisfy their demands and desires and are bidding more and more for what has turned out to be a limited and insufficient supply of goods.
I suggest that this government should have embarked at least two years ago on a program which embraced the following four policies: first of all, a greatly accelerated program for training the skilled workers needed to carry out an expansion program to meet the increased demand for goods both at home and in the export markets; second, an immigration policy which would attract the number of skilled workers required to supplement the insufficient number being trained by our technical training schools.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

I will answer your question at the conclusion of my remarks.
The third step would be to create incentives encouraging industry to increase productivity and thereby lower the cost of manufacturing goods and the selling price. The result of this step would make our manufactured goods more competitive and in turn increase sales in the export market. The final step would involve a policy of providing industrial loans at reasonable interest rates so that Canadian industries could expand and 
keep pace with the world demand for products. This would of course reduce inflationary pressures at home.
These policies must be introduced even now so that this country can meet the problems associated with inflation and growth in a positive rather than negative manner. If the government refuses to take these steps it will soon realize it has blundered and pushed this country into another recession similar to the one which occurred in late 1956 and early 1957. When we took office we found that inflation was already well on its way and it took us some three to four years to pull the country out of it. I urge the government to throw away its sterile and negative policies, which is all they seem to be able to think of today, and adopt positive policies such as those I have outlined.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps the government has made a small move in the right direction but as yet the results have not been sufficient. Mr. Chairman, I asked a very simple question. I did not quote the exact figures involved, but the program followed by this government resulted in an increase in the immigration of skilled workers amounting to three times what it was in 1962. Is it not a fact that the policies followed by the former government were such that the immigration of skilled and other workers
September 9, 1966

shrivelled between 1958 and 1962 from 200,000 per year to less than 70,000 per year?

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
That is a very easy question to answer and I am pleased that the minister has posed it. The former Liberal government which went out of office in 1957 had been warned of the impending situation by the so-called hidden report early in 1957. In spite of that fact and as a result of the negative and sterile policies of that government we experienced a recession that was well launched by the time this party formed a government, and it was not until 1961 that we were able to pull the country out of this difficulty. In spite of the former government's mismanagement and negative policies we were able to bring the country out of this recession and create a momentum that has not yet ended.
The problems faced by Canada during that recession were not related to the lack of skilled workers but rather to the lack of jobs. In contrast, within the last two years it has become apparent that there is a lack of skilled workers. We have unfortunately not been able to do anything about this shortage in the past two years because we have not been in office. I assure the minister that we will be back in office soon and something will be done to alleviate the problem.

earn his salary, which obviously from his own words he is not earning at the present time.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to reply to the hon. member by blaming Tweedledee or Tweedledum back and forth. The fact is that while the opposition was in government the same mistakes were blamed on them, and I will not blame the opposition any more than I will criticize the minister. I think the minister did the best he could with the concepts he was given by his department. What I will take up with the minister, if I can debate with him, is that his staff, those keen young fellows who 30 years ago were great followers of J. Maynard Keynes who propounded a new concept of economics, have forgotten that times have changed.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: The problems are still the same.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
I heard the hon. member for Northumberland say that inflation means we have too much money chasing too few goods and therefore if there is inflation there is too much money and too few goods. This is nonsense. It is quite possible to have inflation at a time of unemployment and with a surplus of goods. I have gone over the speech of the minister and I believe that many of the concepts on which he has based his policy are the same as those used by the Conservatives and the N.D.P.
First, there is the concept of supply and demand. Ever since the time of Adam Smith people have supplied goods and others, the consumers, have had to make a rational choice as to how they will spend their earnings and what goods they will buy. This is a presumption. The fact is that today the consumer does not exercise his own demand. Since the time of Adam Smith, and in fact since the time of John Maynard Keynes, we have had advertisements and psychological promotion. We now have the television medium and we have the use of every conceivable emotional method to try to get people to buy goods. The people who exercise control over promotion are the same people who manufacture the goods. In other words, the economists and, I dare say, to this day even the minister's staff, presume that if a manufacturer decides there is too much soap on the market he will stop manufacturing it and transfer his money to the manufacture of shoes or another commodity. This is nonsense; he does not do that. What he does is to

September 9, 1966
Supp ly-Finance
put another $50,000 or $100,000 into promotion and he says: Do not buy that other soap, it has too much suds; buy mine, it has no suds. Eventually he may even say: Eat soap, it is good for you.
The manufacturer and the supplier are one and the same person. They control both supply and demand, which alters the situation. There is supply and competition among the suppliers as to who will create the greatest demand. The supplier controls the demand through the powerful media of advertising. Does the supplier discriminate with regard to demand? Does he say, you should not buy a Cadillac, to someone who has an income of $2,000 a year? He does not. He does not care what the buyer's earnings are. He says: You must have a colour television set. He makes sure that the child goes home and says: "Daddy, are we so poor that we cannot have a colour television set? Everyone has a colour television set." Very powerful but insidious methods are used, and therefore to presume that there is such a thing as demand is incorrect.
Another phrase was used in the speech to the effect that a restriction of the money supply will dampen expansion. Normally this would be the case. In days gone by, when a manufacturer decided money was too tight he would not increase his sales or his production facilities. However, this does not happen these days. The supplier does not care as long as he can sell. If he thinks he can promote a profit he will sell at any price. He knows everyone else is in the same position and he does not care if he pays 10, 12 or 15 per cent for it. He will do it if he thinks he has the sales.
I read the following this morning in one of London's daily newspapers:
Imperial Chemical Industries Ltd., Britain's biggest industrial combine, yesterday announced lower profit and plans to raise a $180 million loan at a rate of interest that will yield more than 8 per cent.
A restriction was put on credit by the U.K. government, but whether a company has to pay 8 or 10 per cent does not matter. An entrepreneur will borrow money to expand his plant. He does not care about the cost he pays because he knows he will be able to pass it on.
Another statement made in the speech was that we are producing all we can. This is a comment that is sometimes made and I will not question it. I think it is the minister's

department which should question that concept. But are we really producing all we can? We are not. I have no hesitation in saying that most of our industries can produce another 40 per cent.
Many comments have been made about the high demands of labour. I do not think that is the case. A labourer will work as hard as a man can work because he wants to produce. However, he also wants to see the result of his production. It is all very well to say that labour is not producing. The fact is that labour looks at junior and senior executives and finds that they come to work at 10 a.m., have long lunch hours from noon to 3 p.m., have club memberships and live high oil the hog with diner's club memberships and everything else. That is not true. Management works during hours when labour does not see them. The trouble is, however, that there is no leadership. We lack the quality of leadership in our country. Management has to pull up its socks. It has to indicate to the workers that there is some purpose in the work of the company and that it is not all going to waste.
We are hampered, of course, by the method of distribution of shares in today's corporations. The management class is not really concerned about dividends. The whole share structure has been so diversified that management can sustain itself almost indefinitely until there is a strong movement among the shareholders to throw management out. We have to think about reforming these methods. We can produce a lot more.
There is also a presumption that both labour and management will deny themselves greater profits and will do what is good for the country. I have been in business myself and I can tell you that a businessman will admit he has only one interest and that is to make money. This is his immediate concern and he is shortsighted in that way. He knows that if he wants a greater profit he must demand and get a higher price. Labour takes the other point of view and asks for higher wages. Therefore, to presume that management and labour are angels is wrong. They are not angels; they are human beings and they will act in this way.
If we are to put forth policies calling for voluntary restriction we are not going to be very successful. There is also a presumption that savings flow back. The phrase used in the speech was that savings will flow into industrial development. Savings do not flow into industrial development. Savings are those moneys that one scrimps for and does
September 9, 1966

without in order to gather. You do not gamble this kind of money. This is security money. If you happen to make some easy money-dividends or profits-that is the type of money that goes back into investment but not savings.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
How much do we have in savings? It was estimated we had about $16 billion in savings. After the Rothschild and a couple of other robberies, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics upped its estimates and it is said we now have savings amounting to $27 billion. This is not being used for investment. We do not gamble it because the Canadian is not the type to gamble. If you presume that if you enforce more savings you are going to have more money into ventures is to eliminate the risk. To assume that we are going to expand our savings when we introduce insurance measures and social measures, and that they will mean less use for savings in the future, is wrong.
I believe that what we should do to induce money into ventures is to eliminate the risk. This is the Canadian Development Corporation idea, and I feel we have to get along with that. I am rather worried about the reduction in education grants. I am worried because I do not believe it is proper, reasonable or feasible to presume that when a student interrupts his education he is going to pick it up again. There are human factors that enter into a consideration of this problem. A student may get a job or get married when he interrupts his education and the chances of that person picking up his education again are rather remote. I feel that the danger of injury to the nation as a result of this course is greater than the savings that might emerge.
I believe the minister is correct in saying that we are going to improve and increase our grants to the provinces. I hope that these conferences will not hinder the education program or the scholarship program. I feel that the actions of the minister are going to be successful, according to what I have heard this morning about the market. It appears to me that we may level off.
I am not going to say these policies are not going to be successful. I think we will probably put a brake on the inflation. All I am saying is that we are going to go through this situation every four or five years unless we conduct an examination of our whole economy. No matter whether it is this government or any other government, we are going to
Supply-Finance
face this situation over and over again, with a constant need for immediate solutions without the time to delve into these problems in depth. We will be faced, as we have been faced this time, with a declining stockmarket. People borrow money on the stocks they own. The banks will advance an amount equal to 75 per cent or 80 per cent of the value of the stock. When the market drops the people have to come up with more money. When there are lay-offs and there is no place to dispose of assets the people may be forced to sell their stock. At any time there could be a panic. I do not believe it will happen this time; in fact, I know it will not. We have survived. However, this situation will occur again.
The question is, why should we keep putting ourselves into this position all the time? The restrictions the government is going to impose upon itself in connection with capital spending will, I feel, have an influence. I hope that everyone does not start pulling in their horns. I believe that expansion is something we should be promoting. I do not like restriction. I think it is a negative approach.
Let us consider the housing market. I believe the minister did mention it and referred to the high cost of housing. I have been in this business 18 years and I can show the minister figures to prove that in 1951 we were paying $10.30 per square foot for house construction. I can show figures to prove that today, 15 years later, we can build houses for around $9.73 per square foot. You see, we have very little use for carpenters today. A lot of the components are pre-cut. Window frames and door frames are pre-cut; kitchen cabinets are assembled ready to instal as are stairways. The technique has improved. However, the cost of land has gone up from $1,300 to $3,000 per lot.
The demand is there for houses and it is going to increase as long as people have to have a place to live. They want to pay a reasonable price, and if we do not provide accommodation somebody else will. You cannot remove the demand by saying there is no supply. The demand is there. They want a house or an apartment and they want it at a reasonable price. The price of land has gone sky-high, first, because it is a wonderful ploy for speculators. Second, and possibly more important, land is used as a hedge against inflation. If you put money into land you are going to get good money for good money. If you put money into mortgages or bonds you will get cheaper money for your good money.

September 9, 1968
Supply-Finance
More and more people are hedging, and I include investment funds, union funds and others. They are investing in land without any intention of building but are holding it as a hedge against inflation. Land has taken the place of gold and diamonds for this purpose; it is better than anything else.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
You have the normal pressure of more people moving into the urban centres and you cannot increase the supply of people without increasing the supply of places for them to live. The type of action I should like to see in connection with the problem the minister mentioned would be reform measures in the taxation field to remove the speculative aspect on land. This can be done by reform in municipal, provincial and federal taxation. I should like to see the hedge against inflation removed as a pressure against land. I believe it would be much more reasonable to urge these people to buy government bonds, and this could be done if the government would attach an escalator clause to them so that the return would increase as the cost of living increased. In other words, if a person bought a bond for $100 he would be sure of getting $100 for it in ten years' time. This would remove the pressure from land.
The minister in charge of housing has just left the chamber, but he could do a lot to expand the supply of land by encouraging the supply of services, by using new ideas for sewers and other services. I have told the minister before that by one little change in the National Housing Act he could reduce the cost of land. I believe this could be done by paying the first draw on the mortgage when the builder has picked up the title to the land rather than when he has the roof on the house. This would enable builders to develop small parcels of land by themselves. This would leave the high cost land to speculative developers, the developer who in order to make money has to put up big money. They are the things we should look to, the solution being not to restrict but to expand.
One remark in his speech which struck me was that we would never have as good a standard of living as that in the United States. This exemplifies our attitude, and it is too bad. I ask, why not? We have more resources, more gas, more electrical power. We have a monopoly of uranium in the world. We have the seaway now extending to the centre of our nation. We have hard-working people. We have everything except the necessary spark. What we as a party should

be doing is promoting the greatness of Canada rather than admitting or saying that we are always going to be second. Why not try for first place.
In conclusion, I hope that the parliamentary secretary will convey to the minister the content of my remarks in this vein: that I think he has done as good a job as he could do with the advice he has been given and the emergency of the situation. Granted, he could not investigate all of the points I have mentioned and delve into them fully and then come up with a solution, because it might be too late. But I think he did the right thing in this immediate measure, and I should like the parliamentary secretary to tell the minister that now is the time when we should be looking carefully into our fiscal policies so that the next time this situation occurs we will be prepared.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have just seen the hon. member for Lotbiniere and he is perhaps glad that I am going to speak in this debate. I am going to prove to this committee that the remarks just made by the hon. member for York East in respect to publicity and advertising in Canada are somewhat along the line of thinking of the hon. member for Lotbiniere when he said that the poverty in this country is due in large measure to the over-advertising that we have. For example, people spend money on things they should not buy but are influenced to do so by television advertising, and the situation has reached the point where people are buying more than they can afford. The hon. member supposed that this accounted for the poverty which exists in this country, and this government has now declared war on poverty.
I would ask them how they explain the situation in India, which is a poorer country than Canada and does not have any advertising. There are numerous countries in the world which have no publicity or advertising and are poorer than we are.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: May I say that I did not say that was a good thing. I said that it was a reality of life that control over demand does not lie with the individual. I did not say that was good or bad.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
I was continuing the line of thinking in light of what the hon. member for Lotbiniere had said. I think the television station in Quebec city, CFCM-TV, took care of that in an editorial after the broadcast when they hoped that the free
September 9, 1966

publicity received by the hon. member for Lotbiniere would not result in his constituents being any poorer.
We are now facing a series of declarations from all sides of the house, but what concerns me most is what the minister said yesterday about the need for preventing inflation. What he said amounted to nothing less than the birth of a monster of his own creation.
I should like to bring to the minds of government members the date of May 18 last year when the former minister of finance brought in a measure on which I commented and as a result he called me at that time a "so-called prophet". The only thing I am sorry about is that the former minister of finance is not now sitting across the way, but there are very few Liberals here today.
Let me recall to the government my words at the time. When the amendment to the Bank Act was brought in reducing the reserves of the chartered banks from 8 per cent to 7 per cent, I told the government at the time that it was an election measure and that immediately after the election credit restrictions would follow. In the middle of the summer of 1965 the government did take measures to slow down construction enterprises and plans. The minister admitted in his own statement that in the middle of the summer last year the government slowed down construction programs. He said further that these measures were not sufficient.
At that time the then minister of finance, the present hon. member for Davenport, told me that I was trying to prophesy something and he called me a "so-called prophet". Two of my prophecies have been borne out. We did have an election in the fall and immediately following the election credit restrictions were imposed. These led up to the present situation and the drastic measures now proposed.
The measures announced yesterday by the Minister of Finance are a living paradox. One day the government announces a war on poverty, but from the minister's speech we are wondering how the government will go about waging that war. It is not a war on poverty in view of the issues we have now; it is a war on the poor that we are waging. We are still operating under this D.D.T. system *-debt, deficits, taxes.
This party has been blamed in the past. Some Liberals went around during the last election and in 1963 saying "Beware of Social Credit; beware of inflation". Who in the Sam Hill is bringing about inflation now, the
Supply-Finance
members of the Social Credit party or the Liberal government across the way?

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: And Premier Bennett.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: I have nothing to do with Premier Bennett, but I very distinctly remember there being a socialist government in Saskatchewan and even the rats would not live under it but moved to Alberta.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Only the rats?

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Some provinces have expanded and I have nothing to say against their administrations. But one thing I do know is that provincial governments as well as municipal governments and individuals depend on the monetary policies of the federal government. When these policies are not quite correct and need amendment and shining up, they do not get it. These policies need modernizing. We have today the same situation we faced in 1928 prior to the great world economic crisis.
In 1956-57, when the Conservative government took over, the Liberal government left us on the doorstep of an economic crisis. The Conservatives left us a similar situation in 1962 and in 1966 we meet once more a situation similar to that of 1957. The Tories might say that they coped with the situation. They made a big fuss about the Coyne affair; yet immediately after the election of 1962 credit restrictions were imposed. Coyne was right after all. That was an open admission that Coyne was right.
A fuss was made about this in 1961. People said: Do not apply tight money policies; let us conclude the election first and then you can put them on. Coyne went out and Rasminsky came in. Then we had the 1962 election with credit restrictions in the fall.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, when we look at the measure presented yesterday by the Minister of Finance, we see the following:
Speaking generally, Canadians have been very impatient to get on with very many things both directly and through their governments and now we are paying the price for trying to do too much all at once.
I say that we are not doing enough. It is not that we are doing too much. How can we conceive of such contradictions? How can we compromise, by cutting down credit restrictions? On the one hand it is said that we do not produce enough, and when one turns the page we are told we are producing too much. The small industrialist is blamed, as is the

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance
businessman, because both want to sell goods. That is their job. The job of the manufacturer is to manufacture. The job of the government is to administer, to see to it that the goods, production and services reach the consumers, so that they fill the needs of the consumers.
It is not production that is missing in the economy of this country. The hon. member for York East said that we have lots of wheat in Canada. We have lots of oil, and practically the whole world's deposit of uranium. We have 85 per cent of the world's supply of asbestos. We have natural resources in abundance, even to the extent of pure drinking water, which possibly is one of our greatest natural resources.
We have a smaller population than the United States, yet we have a lower standard of living than that country. The Minister of Finance says that we cannot have the same standard of living, and adds: "The people must tighten their belts".
. What kind of reasoning is that, Mr. Chairman? The natural resources are not missing, nor is the will to produce on the part of the Canadian people. It is purchasing power that is lacking. Yet the government imposes credit restrictions and taxes. How does the minister expect to lower the costs of production by imposing additional taxes? When he said that by the middle of last year it was evident that costs and prices were rising rapidly he should have included, in brackets, the 11 per cent tax on building materials as a contributing factor.
In the summer of 1965 the government cut back on its construction program, urging others to do the same. But the minister said that that was not sufficient. He also said as reported at page 8213 of Hansard:
We cannot all get what we want and do what we .van t, and if everyone tries there is going to be an sxcessive rise in prices and in costs because right aow the country just could not, no matter how nard it tries, produce enough to meet all the demands.
This, Mr. Chairman, is absolutely false.
Some time ago I heard arguments about bringing skilled immigrants into this country. Yet the government cut off 10,000 student loans which would have produced skilled workers in one, two or three years. The government is going against the logic of its own argument, if one can call it logic. If the government wishes to invest in human capital, to develop skilled workers, let it provide the means for the necessary schooling to

produce skilled workers. That will not be done by imposing credit restrictions.
This government will probably be known as the dancing government. It will be called the tango government-one step forward, one sideways and two backwards. Ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare what he thinks of that. I have never seen a government which has sidestepped, somersaulted and jumped over issues as this one has. This government has blackmailed the Canadian people into accepting its measures. Does it think that the people are going to swallow this measure that easily? Oh no, no, surely not. The Canadian people are broadminded enough and awake enough to notice that the means of production are here, and that they can buy what is produced.
Will imposing new taxes help matters? We shall probably lose another part of our external trade, because our competitive position in world markets will suffer because of the imposition of new taxes. One may ask the members of the former Conservative government about pulpwood, and about what happened when taxes were imposed. There was trouble. The Liberal government will be faced with the same trouble.
I heard the hon. member for York East, but I do not know where he got his figures when he was speaking of savings. The government thought that $16 billion of savings was hidden in stockings and cellars. The hon. member said that after doing a little research it was suggested that that figure should be increased to $27 billion. How is it possible, then, to reduce this purchasing power? I believe the figures were obtained from the governor of the Bank of Canada to show that the total cash in Canada is approximately $2-J billion, with an additional $18 billion being represented as purchasing power in the form of credit. I hope that these figures are correct, and I hope the hon. member knew what he was talking about.
