speechtext: Do you?

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member always makes interjections from his seat.
If those figures were obtained from a newspaper, they may not be right, because the newspaper may not be correct. If the minister was trying to cover up mistakes, he was certainly not helping the cabinet, because he is tearing it apart. Probably he was not trying even to speak for himself, but instead, was speaking for some back-seat string pullers, whose puppet the Minister of Finance is.
September 9. 1966

The minister may be pale; he may lose his smile; he may lose his skin-but he will still go along with these people I have referred to. They organize the world as if it were a game of chess.
I know that this inflationary situation is one that faces the whole world. But because it is a world situation, I think we ought to set an example of trying to combat it logically, instead of following others as if we were a herd of sheep following one shepherd. In 1928, before the crash came, the situation was also world wide. It must be remembered, as the minister said, that we are in danger of having a boom-bust affair. Normally when you have a boom in progress, you do not stop it. Usually you kick somebody in the rear end for not moving fast enough. Right now the government is hitting the country on the forehead, trying to stop the boom.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I can take the minister around the country and show him where there is unused production capacity, not because goods cannot be manufactured but because people cannot purchase them. Inflation occurs when the balance between production and over-all purchasing power is uneven. Over-all purchasing power should be sufficient to buy the total production of a country and as productivity increases more purchasing power should be made available to every individual.
This is the job of the minister. He should not kick industry because it is trying to sell its products. That is the job of industry-to sell products. The job of the hon. gentleman is to finance and administer. I know that he has not, so far at least, proposed the devaluation of the dollar. That came about in 1962 under the Conservative government. I am a teacher of physics, or at least I was, and I think I should go back to teaching physics.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
We do not propose the devaluation of our units of measure or length. Countries which have to import timber from Canada do not cut down a 12-foot plank to 11 feet and pay for 11 feet. A cord of wood is always the same size. A mile, whether in England or in Canada, is always 5,280 feet. A yard is always three feet. No one alters that. A pound is always 16 ounces, as anyone who goes into a store knows, and if a shopkeeper fools around with his scales he is sent to jail.
Supply-Finance
How is it possible to change another unit of measure, the purchasing power of the dollar, which is after all a measure of value? If we attempt to change the ordinary measures of length and weight, we get into trouble. But because we do not control our financial system we are forced to permit a variation in the value of this other Canadian unit of measure, the dollar. Someone is controlling it; somebody is influencing it, and it is not the Minister of Finance.
This means that the Minister of Finance is little more than a puppet. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has been obliged to defer his medicare plan to another year. I sympathize with the hon. gentleman; he did not seem very happy today. But he will get used to it-one step forward, two steps sideways and two steps backward. We should all take care lest this system lead the Canadian people another kind of dance-a war dance.
I have been reading some of the statements made yesterday by the hon. member for Three Rivers. Knowing his background, I would agree that he has a perfect right to say what he said.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: I have not said anything about the hon. member yet. I merely said I had read his speech.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: On a point of order. My city is called Trois-Rivieres, not Three Rivers.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
Let me give the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres a little grammatical lesson on that. There is no mistake in a proper noun. Look up your grammar on that. But I am quite ready to agree with the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, if it will help him-though whether you like your water in English or French, it is still the same place. What is more important to me is the guy who represents that place. This is what he said:

When I heard the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) tell us that the government stated, without any evidence, that we had reached our maximum production, I asked myself some questions. I told myself that explanations should have been given, of course.
Right. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) gave an explanation. What was it?
I think the minister meant our maximum production with the means at our disposal right now.

September 9, 1966
Sup p ly-Finance
He thinks, he believes, he is not sure. The minister is not sure, nor is the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres. Who is, in that case?
What is the meaning of "we have reached our maximum production"? I indicated a while ago that this was false, Mr. Chairman, and that if we afforded opportunities for our industries to produce according to their capacity and as they thought fit in this country, our gross national product would have doubled in two years.

I can well understand the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres speaking that way. He is a very logical man. Right now, his political colour is white-independent. But if he swerves too far into the Liberal left he comes out a silly, pink colour and I would advise him to stay on his own feet, not try to cover up mistakes of the government. He is a good hearted man, a kind man; I know that. But that will not help the government at all.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: On a question of privilege, might I direct a question to my hon. friend? It may be that I am becoming a heretic but does he not think this is because I have a mad sight in front of me?

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
I am glad to find that somebody in this house has been influenced, though for my part I think the influence is coming more from the left of the hon. member. He is turning it from white to pink, but at least I can congratulate him because he is the only one who has ever been influenced in this house. I, for my part, do not need anyone to influence me because I am convinced of the soundness of my opinions.
The minister is forced to confront the need for taking measures against inflation because of his stupidity in maintaining an obsession with outmoded financial and fiscal policies. I do not see why he should try to maintain the system which has led us from chaos to crisis, and from crisis back to chaos.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Does he believe it is because of the outmoded socialist system in Britain that they are having their troubles over there?

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: They have a leader with guts over there, anyway.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext:
I am not saying they are likely to find a better solution, but unless Canada or any other country chooses to arrange its fiscal and economic machinery

along different lines we shall always be facing the kind of situation which confronts us now.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Will the means and methods that have brought us bankruptcy, chaos and crises, lead us to success and prosperity? I say you have to change your methods of operation, and change your ways and means, but the minister will have to tell some of his back-seat string pullers to leave the scene, cut the strings and let him act as he should-not as a politician, not as a puppet for some high financiers, but as a statesman, looking not to the future of the next election but to the future of the next generation.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: You are quoting Duplessis.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: Maybe the hon. member for Lotbiniere will have something to say himself.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: That is not one of your finds. Maurice Duplessis said that: Next election, next generation.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: That is quite true. Maurice Duplessis may have said it, but he was still premier of the province of Quebec for 16 years and he must have had some good in him.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: You don't have to be very bright to think along the same line as Duplessis.

speechtext:
To continue, Mr. Chairman, I wish to give the Minister of Finance notice that when we return after October 5 to deal with the Bank Act revisions in committee, we will have a lot to say and many questions to ask concerning this situation. Before any members of the government go out on public platforms again and say, "If you let the other guy in you are going to have inflation," I would remind them of a fellow named Dupuis who hollered and yelled and paid thousands of dollars for television time, and who said, "If you are going to vote Social Credit you are going to have inflation." He has been defeated since and now is back home.
Now we have a Liberal government and there is inflation. But Dupuis had been told to say that, the same as the Minister of Finance
September 9, 1966

was told to write the speech he made yesterday. Maybe somebody else wrote it for him, but he delivered it and he will have to take the comebacks on it. In conclusion, I hope the minister will not retain this tight money, belt-squeezing attitude toward the Canadian people but will introduce measures in the near future to open up better prospects for them.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, rather suddenly everyone in Canada is concerned about inflation and the rising cost of living. It is an important problem but it is not a new one. I recall speaking in this house in 1963 on the evils of inflation, and particularly the injustice to those on fixed incomes, and in 1964 putting a question on the order paper with regard to methods of controlling inflation while maintaining full employment. Undoubtedly, however, the present widespread interest in the problem is due to the fact that during the last year the pace of inflation has increased.
Since 1949 the cost of living in Canada has increased on the average by about 2.7 per cent a year. During the last year it has gone up about 4 per cent. Therefore we should welcome the restraints announced by the Minister of Finance last evening.
It is interesting that among large trading countries Canada has maintained the value of its currency and the purchasing power of its money better than any other country, with the exception of the United States. The July, 1966, monthly economic letter of the First National City Bank contains a table summarizing clearly the depreciation which has taken place in major world currencies in the last 10 years, and I would like to refer to this table to show what our record has been.
In this period of 10 years United States currency has depreciated by 1.7 per cent on the average per year, Canadian currency by
1.8	per cent, United Kingdom currency 3 per cent, French currency 4.6 per cent, the currency of the Federal Republic of West Germany 2.2 per cent, that of the Netherlands 3 per cent, of Norway 3.3 per cent, of Denmark
3.8	per cent and of Sweden 3.6 per cent.
In comparison with other countries our record in Canada is excellent, so it is nonsense to say, as the Leader of the Opposition said earlier today, that inflation is running wild in Canada. It is not only nonsense, it is irresponsible. And to say, as did the hon. member for Northumberland earlier today, that there is to be a final increase of at least 30 per cent in railway wages is also, in my
Supply-Finance
opinion, irresponsible. If such a speculative statement has any effect at all it will fan the fires of inflation. The hon. member knows very well that the final railway settlement will depend upon negotiation, and if that fails, arbitration. To forecast the outcome at this time is not only irresponsible but improper.
It has also been proven time after time that the seaway settlements earlier this year were based on the fact that many of the men were part-time workers and there were special factors involved which form no precedents for the railway, or any other labour dispute.
All of us know how often N.D.P. members urge us to follow the socialist policies of certain of the Scandinavian countries. It should therefore be of great interest to them to read the figures I have given which show that in Scandinavian countries the cost of living has increased much more rapidly than it has in Canada and the United States. We cannot say that our trading position is undermined by inflation, or that the prosperity of the average Canadian is in danger. The cost of living has gone up in Canada. However, wages and salaries and social security benefits have gone up even faster. In point of fact, despite high costs the prosperity of Mr. and Mrs. Canadian is at a record level.
There is in fact no sudden crisis, but restraints are necessary and all hon. members should welcome and support the action announced by the Minister of Finance last evening. For while there is no sudden crisis, the federal government must accept responsibility for maintaining the value and the purchasing power of our money. Subsections 14 and 15 of section 19 of the British North America Act give to the federal government exclusive legislative authority over banking, currency, coinage and the issuance of paper money. Is there anyone in this house who would suggest that while the federal government has exclusive authority to issue money it is without legislative authority to take appropriate action to maintain the value and the purchasing power of the money it issues?
Under our constitution parliament, by properly drafted legislation, clearly has the exclusive legislative jurisdiction to maintain the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar. It is true that such legislation may possibly affect property and civil rights within the provinces. However, such conflicts are not unusual, and it is well established that in the event of any such conflict the federal legislation must prevail.

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance
Can we maintain the value of our currency without throwing our economy into a recession? That is a good question and one that economists have debated at length. It is the reason why the Minister of Finance and the government must avoid radical measures such as those advocated by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, and must proceed slowly and with care.
The favourable reactions today on the stock markets of the world reflect confidence in the action announced by the minister last night.
Professor Clark some years ago in his authoritative report on old age security said this:
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The maintenance of a stable price level in the coming decades is, in my opinion, as in that of many other economists, compatible with practically full employment ... I believe the achievement of these two goals, though difficult, is highly desirable and feasible most of the time, hut, such is the nature of economics, I cannot prove it in any conclusive way. The attainment of these goals will require co-ordinated government and central bank policies more vigorously directed to these ends and a greater degree of restraint on the part of some strategically placed trade unions and business executives than has been exhibited in Canada and the United States in the past decade. The initial and prime responsibility for achieving these goals must rest primarily with the federal government, but it is not likely to succeed fully without full support from labour and business leaders.
The views of the Economic Council of Canada are to the same effect. The desirable goals are high employment, a good rate of growth and stable currency-and they are all important. In a recent article Dr. John J. Deutsch said this:
At the end of the war, the governments of many countries, including those in Great Britain, the United States and Canada, accepted responsibility for the maintenance of high levels of employment. In the light of subsequent events, it is noteworthy that this far reaching change in the role of governments was not matched with an equal concern for the maintenance of the value of money. For some years at any rate the pursuit of expansionist policies designed to promote full employment was an overriding and almost single aim. This onesided emphasis in both monetary and fiscal policy was, of course, the heritage of the great depression and of the long history of business cycles in the 19th and 20th centuries.
Hon. members will recall that not too many years ago we had high rates of unemployment in this country. The former government, headed by the present Leader of the Opposition, time and time again refused to accept responsibility for that unemployment. Members of that government referred repeatedly to high unemployment in the United States and western Europe and said that
[Mr. Wahn.l
Canada was helpless in the face of a worldwide recession.
The present government, on the contrary, has taken the position that even with its open-ended economy Canada can achieve full employment and control its economic destiny, and it is our obligation to do just that. The present government has accepted that responsibility and is achieving that great goal. It is the same with inflation. If we are to eliminate inflation and maintain the value of the Canadian dollar we must believe that this is possible even at full employment levels, and we must accept responsibility for doing that. In his book "The Affluent Society" Professor Galbraith said:
Next only to the virtues of competition, there is nothing on which the conventional wisdom is more completely agreed than on the importance of stable prices. Yet this conviction leads to remarkably little effort and, indeed, to remarkably few suggestions for specific action. Where inflation is concerned, nearly everyone finds it convenient to confine himself to conversation. All branches of the conventional wisdom are equally agreed on the undesirability of any remedies that are effective.
This describes pretty well the speeches of most members of the opposition since last evening-a great deal of talk but so few, if any, helpful suggestions. The problem is an urgent one because in terms of purchasing power the Canadian dollar today is worth about 70 cents as compared with 1949, and 35 or 40 cents as compared with 1939. I emphasize that this is not the result of any sudden inflationary crisis but of a long continued creeping inflation which has been permitted by all governments whatever their political stripe, and particularly the previous government with its large and continued budget deficits.
The consumer price index shows that compared with 1949 we are today paying 43.8 per cent more for our food, 44.3 per cent more for housing, 25 per cent more for clothing, 51.1 per cent more for transportation, 80.7 per cent more for health and personal care, 59.2 per cent more for recreation and reading and, surprisingly enough, only 25.1 per cent more for alcoholic beverages. Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, the exceptionally high percentage increase in the cost of health services emphasizes that the cost of medical care is likely to increase rapidly, whatever method of financing it is adopted. Not so long ago anyone who urged and supported sound money was considered a diehard reactionary. This apparently is no longer true. The clever people, the wealthy people who can hire trained investment advisers to look after their interests can
September 9, 1966

protect themselves very well against the rising cost of living. The people who are hurt by the rising cost of living are the old, the weak and all those who are least able to look after themselves. Professor Clark in his report on old age security said:
Inflation is inherently unfair to those economically or politically incapable of defending their interests. This includes some categories of salaried employees and those on pension-both private and government. Recipients of government old age pensions are in a position to exert some political pressure on their own behalf;-
Many of us know from personal experience that this is true.
-those on private pensions usually have little opportunity and no contractual claim to have their pensions raised to offset inflation since their retirement. Those widows, orphaned children and retired persons who are largely dependent financially on the proceeds of life insurance policies, annuities, interest on government or corporate bonds or other investments of fixed, or nearly fixed, rates of interest, suffer from inflation with no prospect of relief.
Professor Kenneth Boulding has said:
Inflation is a refined method of taking bread out of the mouths of the aged, the infirm, the widows and the orphans.
It is sometimes asked whether any government will take effective action to end inflation, because governments themselves profit immensely from inflation. Inflation sends up governmental tax revenues and makes the burden of their outstanding debt much lighter. Governments have borrowed millions of dollars, and with inflation can pay back not only the interest but the principal of that borrowed money with cheap or deflated dollars.
If you paid $100 for a government bond in 1949 you have now lost $30 in purchasing power and the government has gained $30. In effect it has imposed a $30 capital levy upon you because you were patriotic enough to buy government bonds. Inflation is in fact a tax upon the general public which bears most heavily on those who are least able to protect themselves. Moreover it is a tax which is authorized by no statute of parliament, without the consent of the people or any of their representatives in parliament, and without even an order in council passed by the government. It is a tax imposed by administrative action or lack of proper action. In fact it is taxation without representation, which is something about which all members of this house should be particularly concerned. For this is the reason we should welcome the action announced by the Minister of Finance
Supply-Finance
last evening. Because inflation is such a convenient tax, it will be given up completely only if the people of Canada, through their representatives in parliament and through all the organs of public opinion, insist that the government accept responsibility not only for containing the 4 per cent inflation of the past year but also for eliminating the creeping inflation that has gone on for so long and under all governments.
This is particularly important for a young, underdeveloped country such as Canada. In Canada we are few in number, inhabiting a great area with vast undeveloped natural resources. Our need for developmental capital is almost unlimited; yet there is a world-wide shortage of capital. Nevertheless, with our stable political system and highly developed and efficient banking system we could attract capital from every country in the world if only we could assure investors that the purchasing power of our money will be maintained, and that our currency will not be depreciated.
Many members of the house are concerned about the very large amount of foreign equity capital in Canada. They would like to see more foreign loan capital instead of equity capital. How can we expect this if we propose to pay back loans in devalued dollars? If we can guarantee lenders that our dollars will not be depreciated we will get the loan capital we need, and in time this will reduce foreign control in our business and industry.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Sound money will also encourage increased savings and investments by Canadians in Canada. The traditional copybook virtues of hard work, thrift and honesty are not obsolete. We need them, and we need them far more than do the older, more fully developed countries. But these virtues have been made to seem old-fashioned and have been discouraged by a continuing and creeping inflation.
I welcomed the statement of the Minister of Finance because I took it as a declaration by the present government that here in Canada we propose to have both full employment and sound money, and that the federal government accepts full responsibility for achieving these objectives. I hope that as policy develops, new methods will be applied in addition to those referred to by the minister. For my part I think we should adopt the technique we have adopted in recent years in launching our successful attack on unemployment. We emphasized that an industry by

September 9, 1966
Supp ly-Finance
industry approach with a view to increasing employment in the secondary manufacturing and service industries was selective. However, it has been successful.
Similarly with inflation, some commodities have gone up in price more than others. Some price increases have a basic effect on the economy and have triggered other price increases. We must concentrate our forces to prevent price increases of strategic materials in scarce supply.
In attacking inflation in Canada we must use the rifle, not the machinegun. We should know our target and have good reasons for firing. We have an adequate arsenal in our monetary, fiscal, credit and rationing powers. I think most of us would agree with the minister when he says that we must not rely entirely on monetary measures, and that we also would agree when he says this is not the time for any general wage or price controls. However, we should be prepared when necessary to use all the weapons in our arsenal against selected targets.
In leafing through the Criminal Code the other day I came across a section that makes coin clipping an indictable offence and provides that any one who impairs, diminishes or lightens a gold or silver coin is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for 14 years. Over the years governments in all countries of the world, including our own, have consistently permitted their currency to be depreciated. I think it is time this was stopped. I am glad this government has set an example, and I urge it to continue so that soon we will be in a position to guarantee the people of Canada that our currency can be accepted in full confidence, and that its value and purchasing power will be maintained.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate having a minute or two to take part in this debate. I cannot help but recollect the series of metaphors used by the hon. member for Megantic when he described the Minister of Finance. Perhaps the minister is now thick-skinned enough that he is able to accept such descriptions. As I understand them, the Minister of Finance is a chess-playing, fancyskating shepherd who indulges in tangos, and is a puppet. In view of that combination I am sure the minister has a career ahead of him that will be flexible, to say the least.
The hon. member for St. Paul's, who just resumed his seat, discussed the rise in the cost of living and quite rightly laid great stress on the strength of Canadian currency.

He had a poignant word or two to say about the real sufferers from inflation-the sufferers that we who represent them in the parliament of Canada should keep in mind. He was referring to the people who are on fixed incomes.
The hon. member for St. Paul's mentioned that the increase in the cost of living last year was 4 per cent. I am not going to get into a debate on percentages because I think they can be made to fit almost any argument. However, the figures I have seen show an increase in the cost of living for the last 12 months of 5.5 per cent. Perhaps some expert will point out why I am wrong.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO POSTPONEMENT
speechtext: I think I can clear that question up. The 5.5 per cent figure represents the number of points the cost of living index has risen, which in turn works out to a 4 per cent increase.

speechtext:
As usual, a lawyer from Royal needs a lesson in economics from a lawyer from Toronto. I accept that explanation. I agree that the Minister of Finance is right in some aspects of his speech, but I do not want anyone to believe for one minute that I feel his proposal to cut back on scholarships and on government spending for research is one which meets with the approval of the opposition. Neither do I personally approve of the postponement for a year of the medicare plan.
I think the minister is right in wishing to mobilize the total population of Canada to the danger that faces us. It interests me as a member of this house, and one who takes an interest in the system of parliament and its relevancy to contemporary affairs, to note that on many occasions we debate issues after the events. I acknowledge immediately that the hon. member for St. Paul's discussed the problem of inflation in 1963 and asked a question about the matter in 1964. Surely that has been the exception that proves the rule. I am delighted that the hon. member mentioned the subject, but I think it can be said generally that members have ignored the problem of inflation in their participation in debates in parliament.
It is my submission that Canadian people are starving for candour and frankness. I also happen to believe that they are starving for leadership; but that is a subject about which we would obviously disagree. I also believe that we as political people underestimate the ability of Canadians to take their medicine.
September 9, 1966

The other day I was reading an English publication about problems in the United Kingdom and how the ordinary citizens of that country tried in rather bizarre ways to lend their support to the efforts of the Wilson government to stem the economic crisis. I admit that I was reading an editorial which appeared in Punch, which is not noted as a thoughtful journal' on political affairs. I was struck by the fact however that a good many people in Britain were doing their best to think up ways and means whereby they could aid the government in its plans. One old lady wanted to knit scarves and balaclava helmets. I think she has forgotten it was 20 years ago that they were necessary.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Another gentleman who had investments in the midland mills in Britain said he was not going to sell his shares in the textiles mills because if he withdrew his money the mills might suffer thereby. This is perhaps trifling but it is an example of a mood which I think we must encourage in this country. We must alert the public to the dangers that confront us.
I had hoped that when the minister made his announcement last night some of the more spectacular plans for government spending might have been phased out-I think that was the minister's phrase. I hope that this great triple tower, this defence structure that is about to go up, will be phased out. I cannot see any feature of Ottawa or any landscape that would be improved by this building. There are other aspects of government expenditure that might also undergo a phasing out process.
I wish to speak for a moment about medicare and to offer a suggestion. I was going to presume to become a bridge between differing opinions in the cabinet, but this role is not really one that I can assume. However, I do have this suggestion: We are told that we are to debate medicare in the next month or two and that parliament is to pass a statute on it. There are a great many people in Canada who live on fixed incomes, people in receipt of old age security and old age assistance who will become the pilots or the first phase of the government's medicare program.
As we all know, recent amendments to the social security act in the United States have brought into the medicare plan people in receipt of social security who are over the age of 65. I think this could also be applied in Canada and might be a very good way of augmenting the scheme of medicare for the
Supply-Finance
whole nation. If we could bring into the plan the older people of 68, 69 and 70 years of age, as well as those living on old age assistance who are over 65, we would be keeping our promises to them. I also think we should not postpone the date of July 1, 1967 on which the medicare plan is to start. I think there are very few centennial projects that would attract me more than that the older population of Canada on the hundredth anniversary of our country would be given the benefits of medicare. As I say, this would be a pilot for the massive plan which the government has announced will take place on July 1, 1968. If this modest plan could alleviate the problems faced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, then I would offer it to him without any copyright.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway discussed sacred cows and birth control. I also was interested in the announcement from India that birth control devices were about to be used which would result in fewer sacred cows. I wish this device could be instituted in parliament, because ever since the beginning of this emergency session we have had a good many of them trotting up and down the corridors of this chamber. One of the sacred cows, of course, is that everyone seems to be busy trying to find out whether someone is to the left, to the right, or in the middle. I was rather interested in the railway debate because some of the hon. members on the right voted with the so-called "left" although for different reasons. Nevertheless the sacred cows in that debate were very much in view, and they have been trotting around. One of them is that all the blame should be put on industry. We heard from the hon. member for Megantic that they all live on diners' credit cards and take three hours off for the luncheon period. Some people from industry have used the well worn phrase that if it were not for the incessant demands of labour there would be no inflation and costs could be kept down.
I will trot out my sacred metaphor and say: A plague on both your houses. At this point I will try to be my best left wing self-I am large enough to be both-and say that anybody who has watched the immense profits reaped by industry in this country in the last three years cannot be very surprised at labour,-although they cannot have had the service of economists who are available to a good many other sectors of our national life,-making incessant and I think quite proper demands for increased wages. On the

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance
other hand the sacred cow of compulsory arbitration, or the concept that we must use the free instruments of collective bargaining to solve all our problems, does not appeal to me in the least. I think-and here I will become my right wing self-there is a large area of public or quasi-public employment where some definitive system of adjudication of perfectly natural demands for increased wages must be augmented, without the necessity of a strike which cripples the whole nation.
I have now covered the whole gamut from left to right and perhaps my comments have not been very fruitful. Nevertheless I wanted to make them. May I be allowed to end my remarks with one other appeal to the minister. My first one was a suggestion to grant medicare to our older people. The second one is a plea to the minister to remember that in some parts of this country the problems brought on by inflation and unemployment are not the same as in others.
I recently read a review by the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council on Agriculture regarding that area. I think that all hon. members, be they from the maritime provinces or any other part of Canada, should read this document and digest the startling facts that are contained in it regarding the drastic reduction in the incomes of the farming population of that area. This is statistical evidence of the pressures under which this part of the community lives.
I hope the minister will be flexible enough in his phasing out program to take into account the fact that there are many places in this country where unemployment is still far too high. I admit that this problem is improving and I give credit where credit is due, but unemployment is still much above the national average, dangerously so, and a fixed program of phasing out is not applicable in the maritime provinces. The minister's own Economic Council can bear this out.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I do want to say one other word about the education program. In response to a question of mine this morning the minister stated that the priorities that have been suggested by the premier of Manitoba were not discussed by the Prime Minister because there were political motives behind them. I did not want to tie up the house during the question period with a battle on semantics. If the premier of Manitoba is not indulging in politics, and I use the word in the best sense, and the minister himself is not indulging in politics,

then what on earth are we about in this land? It happens that the first public announcement I saw about the need for priorities came from the premier of Manitoba. If this simple fact is politics, and if the government is so sensitive that an idea which comes from the premier of some other province must be political, then I despair for the nation and for the oncoming needs of that nation.
Now that priorities are fashionable the minister is clasping them to his breast. He is issuing them out over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in a most persuasive interview, I may say. Priorities, therefore, are the "in" thing and because they are "in" the minister is adopting them. Well, the first comment on priorities that gained public recognition so far as I was concerned came from the premier of Manitoba. I am glad the Minister of Finance for Canada is now on the Roblin bandwagon and recognizes, although there is no evidence of it in his speech, that the major priority in this country must be massive help for technological and postsecondary education.

Mr. Chairman, I want to pattern my remarks after the attitude taken by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pilon), who made a concise and very realistic speech which will have a great influence on the next financial measures the minister will bring before the house.
Also, Mr. Chairman, since we are in a mood for congratulations and admiration, I wish to thank and congratulate the minister for his lucid and masterly statement, which is very interesting to read, and I am sure that the parliamentary secretary to the minister (Mr. Chretien), with his good judgment, had something to do with the position he took.
Mr. Chairman, I have only a few remarks to make as I have just said, perhaps to rectify a wrong impression that may have been given the house a while ago by an hon. member opposite, when he said that I was opposed to commercial advertising as such.
September S, 1966

I must say that I have had an opportunity-in the past to speak on the matter and I have been misquoted, for I am of the opinion that commercial advertising is absolutely necessary. However, this afternoon I understood that the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto), in a flight of oratory, expressed opinions similar to those I have aired in the past, and I would like to take advantage of this opportunity today to rectify that impression.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, commercial advertising is a necessity. However, today's concept of commercial advertising exercises a detrimental influence through the media of the radio, television and the press. One wonders how the demand can be so excessive and how prices can increase so exorbitantly.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether we should not inquire, without making violent accusations, into the part played by commercial advertising in this field, for to those in contact with the people, the masses, it is obvious that they are constantly urged by commercial advertising to buy goods which they cannot afford. Among the main techniques used by commercial advertising, three are obvious and easily detected.
First, they use magic enticements. When they want to sell a product, they say: Do you want to have a great life? You will live in dream-like surroundings. They tempt you with a product supposed to be so wonderful that you escape from reality into an unreal, wonderful and dream-like world.
Another technique of commercial advertising is their trading upon people's vanity. To sell a product, for example a hair preparation, we are shown a young man who is unpopular at parties and whom nobody cares to know. As soon as he uses the hair preparation, all the women chase and love him. These are the kinds of techniques used by commercial advertising, Mr. Chairman.
It is easy to say that people are free, but there will always be naive and credulous people and ways will be found to exploit them and I am convinced that commercial advertising, as strong as it is today, gets the better of the small consumer's freedom of choice.
Mr. Chairman, another method used by commercial advertising is to stress the low cost of the product. One hears all the time: You can get this or that at an unbelievably low price. Here are the current formulas: "Ridicously low prices"; "No down payment"; "36 months to pay". The individual enjoys his purchase for one, two or three months and
Supply-Finance
after that come the lawyer's letter, proceedings, impounding, even the Lacombe Act which forces people who no longer can afford to fulfil their obligations to deposit their salaries at the office of the clerk of the Magistrate Court. That applies to cases in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, I wanted to point out those three methods which exercise a harmful influence, as I said earlier.
And the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) knows how much the psychological factor is important in political economy; it is precisely those things which should be stressed sometimes to explain the economic events which cannot be explained except by great theories which ordinary people are not able to assimilate.
That is the reason why, Mr. Chairman, I wanted to call the attention of the house to those questions and see if it would not be advisable to study the problem and even to impose restrictions, because commercial advertising is supposed to be a way to promote sales, but today it has become an industry, an end in itself.
In England, a board conducted an investigation on trusts and has just tabled its report. That investigation lasted three years. That board recommended among other things that Unilever Limited and Procter and Gamble Limited reduce by an average of 20 per cent the wholesale price of domestic soap and by 40 per cent the sales costs of those products. The investigation discovered, in fact, that in 1964 those two companies had spent almost 20 per cent of the retail price of domestic soap on sales promotion, particularly in advertising.
People say: prices are going up. Prices are going up because sales promotion is exaggerated. And who pays for the promotion of sales, publicity that is? Here again it is the consumer.
Mr. Chairman, the minister pointed out yesterday in his speech that there is a law against monopolies. I wonder if this law should not be extended so as to include a provision against sales promotion monopolies. Advertising has now come to a point, as I was saying a while ago, where the consumer's freedom to choose is overpowered and I believe that, considered in this light, sales promotion can become a cause of poverty.
I repeat that I am not against commercial advertising in itself, because it is necessary. But in the present context, with its intensity and frequency being increased by radio and

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance
television, it inevitably exercises a prejudicial influence on the consumer and, at that point, the state must investigate and find the necessary remedy to correct the situation.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this debate I would first of all remind hon. members that this is the first item of the estimates of the Minister of Finance. We were dealing primarily yesterday, and are again today, with remarks made by the Minister of Finance in opening discussion of his estimates for our consideration. It is only a matter of a few months ago when the minister presented to parliament a budget which he said at the time would control the inflationary forces which were at work in this country, a budget which he said would bring about a further appreciation of the progress that was being made economically in our country.
Looking at the statement which he has made on this occasion, and thinking back to the utterances that have come from former finance ministers over the years-and I have read most of them going back to the earliest years of Canadian history-I have never seen a more dismal denial of Canada's future than that which we see contained in this document that has been presented by the minister on this occasion.
The first sentence of the remarks of the minister, as reported at page 8212 of Hansard, read in this way:
Mr. Chairman, the fact that the committee and the government regard the threat of inflation as an important and urgent matter is evidence that Canada will not drift into a period of continually rising prices and costs.
[Mr. Choquette.l
The minister and the government opposite were warned months ago of what was taking place in this country, of those things that were contributing more than anything else to the inflationary trends that were robbing the Canadian consumers and the Canadian taxpayers of the dollar value of their wage packets.
The minister ridiculed those on the opposition benches, and when we rose in our places in the house, as is our right and duty, to warn of the dangers that lie ahead the minister and the government opposite threw at us time after time the charge that we were trying to obstruct the orderly business of parliament.
The minister went before the television camera the other night and told the people of Canada that we were trying to do too much in too big a hurry. Does that sound as though there has been obstruction in the House of Commons, Mr. Chairman? Certainly not. This gives the lie to the propaganda that has been issuing forth from the National Liberal Federation headquarters, from government benches, ministerial offices and the offices of individual members who sit opposite. The opposition members of parliament have warned about the dangers of inflation for months now. The government has continually said that it had things under control, that the policies that they were employing would meet and overcome the problems that might face this nation in this regard.
The minister went on in his third paragraph to say that we have had a long and strong economic expansion in the past five and a half years. What an admission to come from hon. members opposite, Mr. Chairman, in view of the charges that they made not so many years ago about the government of that day, about the Minister of Finance of that day and about the actions that were being taken at the time to overcome the depression and recession that resulted from the 22 years of Liberal administration prior to 1957.
As I view the document that was presented to the house and to the nation by the Minister of Finance on this occasion, I cannot help but think this afternoon of a former minister of finance, the Hon. Donald Fleming, who during the years tackled the problems which had been created by many of those who sit opposite and laid the foundation for the prosperity and expansion which has taken place today; and I would say that to the Acting Prime Minister who is in his seat today.

The minister said that the government had kept this policy of restraint since that time, though it had not achieved as much success as he would have liked to see. The Minister of Finance cannot say that he was not warned. When we issued those warnings in the House of Commons we were told we were obstructing.
Canada faces today a crisis in regard to a cost of living which is the highest in the entire history of the country. We have the highest interest rates in the entire history of the country. This is undeniable evidence of the failure of the government to discharge their duty. These are the same gentlemen who, in the years when the right hon. gentleman who is today Leader of the Opposition was prime minister, said of his administraton that it was not a businessman's government. These boys sitting across the way had all the answers. They had the business experience and were going to get this country rolling again. They were going to fight the pitfalls of inflation, the way it eats into the consumer's dollar and into the daily lives of all our people.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
A good deal has been said today about high demand, and the fact that it raises prices. It has not been the great demand for goods in Canada that has raised prices, it has been the taxation policy of the government and the financial policies of the government that have raised prices in this country. The fact that when it presented its budget a few months ago the government opposite saw fit to raise income taxes, has had the effect of lowering the take home pay of the individual consumer in this country. The Secretary of State for External Affairs knows that, as well as I do.
The Minister of Finance reached a state of hysteria that we have seldom seen in the House of Commons when he went on to say: "We have reached a position that is unstable". Have you ever heard of a minister of finance in the entire history of Canada saying that we have now reached a position that is unstable? He went on to say that the present trends just cannot continue for long into the future. There are no plans to alleviate the situation; there are just pious hopes. I say that this nation cannot much longer withstand the rigours of the kind of administration that we have had during the last three years.
Listen to these words in the minister's statement:
We are now producing about all we can in Canada this year. We have excellent market opportunities at home and in other countries. We have again been lucky in getting huge grain crops at a time when grains are in great demand. Our labour force is growing at a rate of a bit over 3 per cent a year and is becoming better educated and trained.
Yet this government, in the face of these optimistic factors is, in the words of the minister, facing a prospect that cannot be described as anything but dismal denial of the future of our nation. That is not all, because the minister went on to say this:
We must also recognize that the average Canadian, although he is a fortunate citizen of the world and can look forward to a steadily rising standard of living, cannot have the same standard of living as the average United States citizen-
An hon. member,-I believe the hon. member for York East,-wondered why. I say to the House of Commons, to the government and to the Minister of Finance that this statement made by the Minister of Finance was an indication to the trained young Canadian citizens in our land to seek opportunities in other lands, because by this statement more harm to the future of this nation

was done than has been done by any other single statement within the recent history of our country. That statement is an absolute denial of faith in young Canadians and is an absolute denial in the future of our country. That is what we are to get from the language of the minister, who is in many respects the first minister, when he talks about the economic prospects of the nation.
We on this side of the house cannot help wondering at the words of the hon. member for Leeds, who drew on all the wonderful qualities of the minister, and who talked of the preparation that the minister has had to come to his present position. An hon. member in this debate mentioned mistakes. May I say that people learn from their mistakes. Do you know, sir, if one were to apply that to the present government, it would qualify as the best educated government in the history of our country?
I recall vividly when it came to office that everyone talked of the 60 days of decision. This government said that in those 60 days it would do more than the former government had done during its entire period in office. That 60 days of decision has changed to 60 days of dismissal, sending the members of the House of Commons back to their own constituencies while the government trims its lamps, hoping that the problem of inflation will somehow disappear, and that all will be well.
The businessmen of this country must wonder at the antics of the government, when they listen to the statement which was made by the Minister of Finance with respect to things that should be done, only to hear him say that those things are not to be done because of the problems that face this nation-that these things will not be done for another six to eight weeks. Certainly, that is hard to understand.
You know, sir, the minister made this very interesting observation:
An alert and informed public opinion can play an important role, as well as those directly involved.
The people of this nation know all about inflation. Every time a housewife goes to the store to buy groceries, clothes or any of the commodities necessary for life, she draws a direct comparison between costs today, and the costs of yesterday. Often, within a week, one can see prices increase a few cents here and a few cents there. The people of the nation do not have to be informed. Those who have to be informed of this are hon. gentlemen opposite.

Not only must they be informed about the problem, but they must make up their minds about what we are to do. As seen from this side of the house, this faceless administration cannot make up its mind on the important problems facing the nation. That is one of the undesirable attributes of the present government.
Referring again to the minister's remarks, he had this to day:
The expansion of the money supply and bank credit has been held in check and interest rates have risen in response to insistent demands for credit.
In recent months the minister has tried to hold in check the money supply. That was not the case a few months ago when the government was pumping every cent it could into the financial system of this country, until the banks held up their hands in terror at what was happening, and the minister had to reverse the process. The government opposite cannot shelve the responsibility that it faces with regard to interest rates. I say this, because of the bank legislation which should have been before parliament before this time and which is still being held up for consideration. By its attitude the government has shown that it favours a high interest rate policy for this nation, and by virtue of that it has encouraged a higher trend of interest rates. In addition, the government has not done anything to alleviate the situation which prevents money being provided at lower costs.
I could go on dealing with other factors in the minister's statement. There was one statement which was of interest to the province of Saskatchewan, and that has to do with the deferring of the medicare program for another year.
This program will cost the province of Saskatchewan in excess of $14 million. All I have to ask the minister is: What has he got
against the province of Saskatchewan?
I want to say something of what the government should have done long ago. This subject has been raised from this side of the house on more than one occasion. It should have brought in a consumer loan legislation program whereby the consumers of this country could purchase the things they need at reasonable rates of interest, as certain consumers can today under the farm improvement loans legislation.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
They could have eliminated the 11 per cent sales tax which they imposed. They could

have set up a department of urban affairs to take care of the problem of urban development in this country. I well recall the way in which members opposite went to people living in urban areas during the election campaigns of 1962, 1963 and 1965 saying: the Tories are the farmers' party; we will do something for those of you who live in the cities and towns. But they have utterly failed to meet this problem of urban development in an effective way.
There is another thing they could do. They could get a prime minister who would put a face on the government opposite, one who would give the government a purpose which we, and all Canadians, could see. If that were done, Canadians would have something to work for and the Minister of Finance would not have to say in the House of Commons that we as Canadians will never achieve the standard of living which our friends in the United States enjoy.
We have the resources. We have a keen, resourceful people. Moreover, as a result of the action taken when the Leader of the Opposition was Prime Minister, we set in motion the greatest technical training program in the entire history of this nation, giving people the opportunity to train themselves for jobs which could build a greater Canada. Yet here we find a government which says it intends to cut back on research spending, to cut back on education. Already in the course of this debate we have seen hon. gentlemen opposite change their minds in this regard. The statement by the Minister of Finance was an ill-considered statement put forward without proper thought.
The other night on television the Minister of Finance made another admission which is even more interesting. He said, in effect, that it was the opposition who were responsible for the troubles we have here in Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is with some reluctance that I interrupt this private debate, but there are a number of comments I wish to make on the baby budget brought forward by the Minister of Finance. During the last two days the minister has taken quite a beating, and on occasion he has had to exit from the chamber to restore himself in order to continue to face the blast.
I hope I can make my remarks with as much equanimity as I can muster despite the anger that must be aroused when one sees the way in which the government proposes to solve the problems of inflation. This budget is a good example of the old adage about generals who are fighting the present war with the weapons and techniques of the last.
I understand that the Minister of Finance is a student of Keynesian economics. Certainly Keynesian economics teach us the use of monetary and fiscal policies and the way we can maintain full employment, and thus are a tremendous improvement over the attitudes and economics that prevailed previously. However, the minister can become too enamoured of this attitude toward our society, and this type of economics does not have the answer to all the problems in our society. Although many changes are taking place, apparently those changes are not within the purview of the minister, nor is he prepared to adopt new attitudes to the new problems that must face Canada.
The problem of the future is that this or any other government that hopes to rule and command the respect of the people of Canada must be dedicated to full employment policies. When such full employment policies are in effect there is a constant pressure on the economy and a great danger of inflation. That danger has to be faced, and I think to some extent we have to accept that part of the inflationary pressure may be a very good thing in moving a society forward along the dynamic path. However, the usual policies of monetary control and fiscal attitudes are not going to be sufficient to contain inflation.
When speaking about his previous budget the minister was full of self-congratulations. He said it had worked. He also felt that his policies would be successful in bringing down
September 9, 1966

the interest rate. Despite the minister's confidence in his policies, the facts of the situation do not warrant such a euphoric attitude.
I would like to quote from the Ottawa Journal of June 22 in which Professor Welsh-ans is reported as saying:
High interest rates are likely to prevail in the Canadian economy for the next ten years-
There does not seem to be any possibility that there will be a let-up in the pressure on interest rates, and certainly the minister's reliance on monetary policy and a free market to bring down those rates is due to fail. He will have to do something in a far more positive way if he is to be successful in this endeavour.
When the minister introduced his 5 per cent withholding tax on industry as a means of curbing inflation it was hailed as a most imaginative approach, but it was quite obvious to most people on the opposition benches that it could not possibly work. If he was serious about containing inflation, if he really wanted to curb some of the growth, some of the steam in the economy, then that 5 per cent withholding loan should have been a tax because it shows up in a company's books as an asset and a company simply borrows against it.
The Monetary Times of June 1966, commenting on the minister's policies said:
Despite Ottawa's pleas for restraint many industries simply cannot afford to slow down.
Budget restraints and Ottawa pleas notwithstanding, Chemcell (1963) Ltd. is going ahead with the $35 million of capital expansion it earlier scheduled for this year.
A report in the Globe and Mail of August 3 said this:
Businessmen have ignored Mr. Sharp's warning of the danger of inflation and disregarded his special tax measures designed to slow down capital spending.
The policies that the minister instituted, the ones he was so hopeful about, simply have not worked. He should recognize this and should recognize the limitations of monetary policy in the kind of economy that we have now. He should also recognize that the fiscal policy he is introducing, although it may be effective in the over-all approach towards containing some of the inflationary pressures, will cause enormous inequities and great injustices to many people.
The minister has called for restraint on the part of government. As a matter of fact he has done more than that. He has just about abandoned every government project that all 23033-525
Supply-Finance
of us had been hopeful of seeing implemented. He is calling for restraint, but it is for restraint on the part of the little man, on the part of the man who has always had to pull his belt in whenever sacrifices had to be made.
We hear that we cannot afford low cost housing in Canada, and that there is not enough money for mortgages. Yet commercial construction spending is soaring. It is not that we have a shortage of goods and services. It is that we have a misuse of goods and services, and that we have an abominable allocation of these goods and services, a distorted sense of values as to what is important and what is not important. Apparently the work that the government does on behalf of the people of Canada is not important. We need increased educational opportunities for our people in order to sustain a long-term growth, in order to see that our people get the advantages of a rich and healthy society, yet we are told we have to cut back on educational grants.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The scholarships that were offered are no longer available. We also have to cut back on research despite the statements made time and time again by the government that they recognize the inadequacy of the research program in Canada, that they recognize that Canada simply must do more in this field in order to progress, that Canada must spend more money on research if only to keep her skilled scientific people in this country and offer them incentives. This program has been set aside; we can no longer afford it.
We cannot afford medicare. Of all programs, there is no justification for the government taking this attitude with regard to medicare. Medicare by and large would be a transfer payment. It would not be a new sum of money taken out of the economy; it is a better way of utilizing the money we are already spending on behalf of the people of Canada. This program has to be abandoned; it can no longer be proceeded with.
Mortgage assistance to our people is a luxury we can no longer afford. We have a mobility program that is trying to increase productivity in this country as a whole by moving people from depressed areas, from areas where employment opportunities do not exist into areas where workers are needed. What do we do? We make sure that we sabotage this program by not seeing that houses are available to the migrants as they

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance
move from one part of Canada to another. This is a fine way of conducting a mobility program; you don't let it get off the ground. Then we complain that there is a disparity between what we are capable of producing and what we are actually producing.
Housing is practically out the window now. In connection with the situation in my own riding I should like to read from the Evening Reporter of July 2. The article is headed "Construction of Houses Takes 50 Per Cent Drop" and it say:
Only half the number of houses have been built in Galt during the first five months of this year compared to a year ago at the same period.
Then from an adjacent municipality the situation is described by the Kitchener-Waterloo Record of May 30 in this way:
50% of Families Can't Buy Home.
At least 50 per cent of the family heads in Kitchener are earning less than $5,000 a year and cannot afford the cheapest new single-family home on the market-
There is a definite need for housing for all families earning less than $5,000 a year.
There is an apparent housing need for those families in the $5,000 to $6,000 category.
The need in the lower income groups is not only for small families but large families as well.
We are not even talking about the poverty-stricken in Canada but the industrial worker who would be considered to be earning a reasonable wage. Yet even the industrial worker finds it almost impossible to buy a home for himself and family. The minister in his statement pointed out that we cannot have everything, and that is quite right. No country, no matter how rich it is, and no people can have everything they want at the same time. But the statement of the minister would ring much truer, would evoke a great deal more understanding and sympathy if we did not read in the newspapers articles pointing out that, while we are talking about what we cannot afford, commercial construction spending is soaring.
It is not that we cannot afford certain things but that the government has decided we are not going to afford them. I would submit to the minister that these things are far more important in terms of priority than the spending going on in other areas. Apparently there is no shortage of funds in other fields. There is no halting of the building of banks and bank offices, despite the fact that Canada probably has more banks in relation to its population than any country in tne world. I do not see any curtailment of the building of service stations. Again, we have
[Mr. SaltsmanJ
more service stations than we need. The report of a royal commission in British Columbia pointed out recently that there should be a moratorium on the building of service stations because they are already overbuilt; but there does not seem to be any shortage of funds for these projects. There does not seem to be any shortage of funds to build tall, air-conditioned office blocks as head offices for companies. I know that air conditioning is very nice, but there is no shortage of office space that would justify this new construction. This is a luxury.
If you are to ask for belt-tightening, should not belts other than those the minister indicated be tightened? If we are to have an increase in the old age pension and a medicare program, obviously these things will cost money because you cannot get things for nothing. Such programs will cost money and taxes will have to be raised in order to provide adequate funds for them. The hardheaded man may very well ask: Where does this money come from? The answer of course is that it comes from the people of Canada; it has to come from them. But it is a question of whose pocket it comes from and for whose benefit the money is raised. I would suggest to the minister that all kinds of taxation possibilities are open to him at this time, especially when he talks about belt-tightening. I understand that exploration in the oil industry is going on apace, despite the fact that our known reserves are adequate for at least 21 years even if we do not take into consideration the oil sands.
I would suggest that the minister look at his policies regarding the depletion allowances to see whether it is fair to give these allowances to companies that really do not need help, when at the same time we are asking the older people of this country to tighten their belts and are telling them that we cannot afford an increase in the old age pension because of inflationary pressures. If we want to afford these things, we can. It does not make any difference in the total distribution picture who gets the money, from an inflationary point of view. The important thing for the government to decide is the allocation of the rewards and resources of this society. The government has made that decision, but I would suggest it has been a very bad decision and is unfair to the older people, the poorer people and those who need housing in this country.
The great challenge facing Canada is how we can take advantage of the dynamic situa-
September 9, 1966

tion that exists, and keep it dynamic instead of slowing it down. The great challenge that faces this country is how we can improve our productivity, how we can manufacture and provide more goods and services and see that they are distributed in a fair and equitable manner. We are not going to do this by relying on the market mechanism and saying that the market will make the decision.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The minister is saying that if people are
willing to pay more they will do so, and if they are willing to bid up prices they are entitled to the commodities at an increased price. We are not going to contain this trend by having the government cut back public expenditures. Surely this cannot be accomplished by a postponement of school and hospital construction, or by the postponement of the institution of a medicare program. The government should not take a first step in this way, or by saying to the older people of this country that we cannot afford to give them an increase in old age pensions.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a question? In which way has he done the things that I have suggested? Surely the Minister of Finance is not so naive as to think that he can call for the curtailment of public expenditures and can indicate that he will approach the provincial governments urging them to use restraint, while at the same time he does not seem to realize what restraint means to provincial governments. After all what sort of facilities do the provincial governments construct? They are the very same facilities about which we are talking.
I would suggest that if the minister is stating that the federal provincial and municipal governments must apply this kind of restraint he is in effect saying to them that according to him the schools, hospitals and libraries which they are building have a very low priority.
When the minister said that he is only deferring medicare and not abandoning it, I wonder whether next year the situation will have changed. I do not believe that it will change in view of the policies which the minister is now introducing. Will the minster not come back to the house next year and say: "I had sincerely hoped that we could have introduced medicare at this time, but just as last year, the year before, and in the last 47 years it is not possible and therefore I hope we will be able to do it the following year." May I suggest to the minister that he could introduce medicare this year if he were willing to call on that small section of our population who are really causing the inflation and say to them: Tighten your belts, and
Supply-Finance
stop this needless and useless construction. However, I do not think the minister is prepared to say this. He is telling us that the sacrifices should be made in the public sector.
I was very interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Lotbiniere who spoke about advertising. I hope the minister listened to this backbencher. Perhaps I should not call him a backbencher because he acts like a frontbencher most of the time. I hope the minister was listening to him because he made some good points. He spoke of the fantastic sums of money which were being spent in this country on advertising, and which are being completely ignored. The minister speaks of restraint. What about restraint being exercised in terms of permissible deductions for advertising? Would this not bring in a nice revenue to the government? If advertising is as potent as people claim it to be, then advertising increases the demand for goods and services. Restraint in this field might be an excellent way of slowing down an overactive economy and at the same time creating additional tax revenues. This has not been suggested by anyone on the government side.
I think this budget will make every Canadian sad. The people of our country will say to themselves: The government has decided that all those things that it promised us and that it said were good will not be possible now because of inflation. They will also say: My government has also decided that the service stations, the new banks and the new shopping centres are far more important; they are more important, when I need medicare or an increase in my old age pension.
I really do not see how the minister has arrived at this set of values. The government may justify it by saying that we cannot have everything all at once and therefore we have to defer these plans until a future date.
May I suggest in closing that the government would be on far sounder grounds if it said to some of the people who are causing inflation in the private sector: You cannot have everything you want exactly when you want it, simply because you can go into the market and pay whatever the market demands for these services regardless of the needs and of the welfare of the Canadian people.
This, Mr. Chairman, is what I suggest is the effect of the budget. It is too much to hope that the minister will listen to the opposition. But I hope he will listen to some of the members of his own party who I am
