Mr. Chairman, I would not like to take too much time and my remarks will be very brief.
I want to talk about the policy of the happy medium, the inflationary system and the means to remedy it without upsetting everything, breaking everything, taxing everyone, in short without increasing taxes of all kinds, so as to enable the government to administer and the people to stop working.
The people must continue to work, to get ahead and to progress. The economy must not be slowed down in any way. There are means to take in that respect and I think that the government does not always see them, does not know the main ones to take. I wish to explain a method to the government, and particularly to the minister, if he would like to try it. Changes will have to be made within his department and that would be for the greater good of the country.
In Canada therefore, in 1966, on this 9th day of September, when the fear of the fight against inflation makes us forget the fight against poverty-we know that a war against poverty has already been declared and we have forgotten it already, because it is said that everyone has tod much money, that the citizens are asking for too much, that there is too much inflation, that the citizens are asking for too much in salary increases, that there is a deficit throughout the country and in everyone's budget. I want to remind everyone that there is no need to get panicky, that God is always with us in all His power and wisdom and that He is at our disposal all the time.
Mr. Chairman, not one of us is afraid that the earth will stop producing tomorrow morning, that we will run short of goods, not even the minister. But we all are terribly afraid of running short of money. The minister is taking steps to restrict credit under the pretext of waging war against inflation. He does it by increasing poverty, by making the poor poorer and the rich richer.
It is the responsibility of the present government to act and restore the national economic balance between production which will reach $56 billion in 1966, consumption which

will reach $38 billion and capitalization which will reach $18 billion.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Before capitalizing over $18 billion, we should guarantee the right to live to 12,600,000 Canadian citizens who have no personal income through their work and their capital and who are dependent on 7,400,000 working citizens and capitalists who divide among themselves production and profits.
Mr. Chairman, in the field of production, there are two kinds of citizens: the employers and the employees totalling 7,400,000.
In the field of consumption, there are the same employers, the same employees and, in addition, 12 million dependent citizens who are consumers and who do not have the personal income to buy the goods and services they need to live.
Thus, we have two types of citizens: the producers and the dependents. If the 7,400,000 producer citizens have a purchasing power by their work and their income, the other 12,000,000 dependents, having no personal income, also have the right to live.
This is a natural and divine right, legally acknowledged in Canadian legislation, namely under Chapter 44 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, and more particularly in the Bill of Rights. However, this essential right has never been acknowledged in terms of dollars; therefore, this right is completely ignored, scrupulously measured, violated even.
For instance, $6 per month, that is 20 cents a day, for a child up to ten years old in his home, that is abnormal, antifamily, antisocial and antihuman, in this plentiful twentieth century.
These same governments pay $65 for a young child in a foster home, and up to $120 in an orphanage.
Due to these conditions, the family budget is completely out of balance, far from the financial and physical realities of the country; taxes imposed by our old-fashioned governments take away the livelihood of a great many of our families and no logical means can be found to stabilize the family budget. Instead of restoring the situation, it is made more confusing and alarming.
Mr. Chairman, what was already in a bad shape, is now in worse shape. There is only one workable national economic policy for Canada, if the political and financial leaders wish to see harmony between production,
September 9, 1966



distribution and consumption, while maintaining the necessary reserves for constant and balanced capitalization.
The numerous strikes at present are proof of the population's dissatisfaction over the lack of national agreement between employers, employees and dependents. All these wage increases for labour, increases in the rates of interest for credit and capital, are responsible for upsetting political and economic balance to a further degree.
However, the greatest cause of national instability and population dissatisfaction remains unheeded.
Management always demands more than labour. Workers receive personal remuneration regardless of the dependents in the various families, the number and age of dependents of different workers: wives and children. It is useless to try to prove that the difference in tax takes care of the situation and balances the two, or that the ridiculously small family allowances re-establish the balance. The most precise calculations of these two adjustments do not even show $10 a month per dependent, but barely 30 cents per day.
All those who are politically influential are favoured by a salary which makes the government family allowances of no consequence to them. Thus the great mass of the people, the five or six million wage-earners, farmers or poor people, cannot fight for their rights unless they form unions. But there again, they are not considered as heads of families. The problem of the father of a family is not discussed in comparison with that of the bachelor.
Mr. Chairman, intentionally or not, production is meant for the consumer first, and then for capitalization.
In speaking of inflation, few know exactly what it is. Inflation throughout the country would be a bad sign. Normal prosperity throughout the country would be proof of good government.
Now, some people say, even members, that inflation was getting to be the normal thing, that there is inflation in the United States and in all European countries and that it is normal for a country to live with such things and to accept an inflationary system. I think it is abnormal, antisocial and antihuman. We must not, and it is nonsensical, accept such a state of affairs in Canada. If other countries deal with this in a certain way, we do not have to follow suit. If someone goes and jumps in the lake we do not have to do
Supply-Finance
likewise. We have other means at our disposal to start the Canadian economy rolling again.
After the war, in 1945, everybody seemed prosperous and nobody talked about inflation. Canadian production was estimated at $12 billion; $10.8 billion were either spent or consumed and about 10 per cent of our production, or $1.2 billion, was capitalized.
In 1966, Canada will produce for $56 billion; $38 million will be consumed and $15 billion capitalized, $15 billion by large companies and $3 billion by private citizens. For directors and shareholders of companies especially, this means a capitalization of 32 per cent of our production, whereas consumption takes up only $38 billion or 68 per cent.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
This goes to prove that there is inflation, as far as capital is concerned, and deflation with regard to consumption, purchasing power and dependent citizens especially, since the 7,400,000 citizens who participate in production have their salaries debated or fixed by the unions.
That part of the population which is experiencing deflation counterbalances for the part which has known inflation continuously since 1945 and, throughout the country, the ills of inflation have passed rather undetected, even though the increasing destitution of most Canadians, especially of the 12 million citizens without an adequate income and their dependents, is not realized.
Mr. Chairman, the inflation of capital is an imbalance. Deflation with regard to inadequate consumption paralyses consumption and discourages any initiative. This is the essential point about the situation of our national economy which is being threatened not so much by partial, occasional and localized strikes, but by this national economic imbalance between incomes, expenses and profits, between individuals, families and companies, between taxes and reserves, between production, consumption and capitalization, on the national level.
In every segment of our economy, strikes are only occasional symptoms of a chronic disease that has been developing over the last 20 years. This is how matters stand. This is the analysis of the situation, the synthesis of our research. Now is the time to make the precise diagnosis which will enable us to find a national, economic and normal balance within the regular framework of monetary, economic and political procedures, adjusted

September 9, 1966
Supply-Finance
according to Canadian, capitalistic and orthodox facts and realities.
Mr. Chairman, every time the workers' wages are increased, every time interest rates and dividends are increased, each time the cost of living is increased for 12 million dependents and those who support them or are responsible for them, a total of 16 million people who have to pay more for all goods and services, without corresponding incomes.
The economic system is always off balance; it should be balanced through a forwardlooking economic policy, taking as an essential basis not labour and capital, but human beings and their essential requirements.
Mr. Chairman, we know the increase in the cost of living and in transportation results from wage increases. There are two methods to ensure that the price figures and the money figures balance: either reduce the prices or increase the contents of the pocket-book.
Social Credit would do both, without hurting anyone while helping everybody.
Under the present system, it is impossible to reduce prices without hurting the producers and to line the pocketbooks without increasing prices.
We have often heard workers asking for wage increases. Why? Because their wages, a money figure, are out of proportion with the price figure on the products. They have grounds for complaints because they have needs which are not met while products are piling up. But if the workers obtain wage increases, such increases are included in the prices. The price figures rise and the spread remains between the price figure and the money figure needed to purchase the products.
The solution would be, Mr. Chairman, to increase the purchasing money without increasing the prices. For that, the extra money should come from a source other than industry. The financial system advocated in our doctrine would do just that. That is what the Creditistes call a national dividend.
On the other hand, the doctrine we advocate also has a monetary mechanism to reduce prices, but without affecting producers, because it would return to sellers the discount which the purchasers would not have to pay.
The two combined together, price reduction and dividend, would be calculated so as to balance the money figure with the price figure.
[Mr. Latulippe.i
Those who persist in saying that one must be employed to be entitled to products on the market are forced to try to employ everyone, while progress reduces employment. As they cannot stop progress, they try to create new needs, so that there might be new jobs. Thus they lead to materialism, or else they apply themselves to war work, to war itself, which is the most efficient means of destroying production and making people work.
The Creditistes want to place progress at man's service, to free man more and more from material concern, enabling him to engage in other human activities, in addition tc the simple productive function.
A dividend for everyone, in addition to being a participation by each and every one to the income of a productive community capital, is also the most direct formula to achieve the right of every human person to share in material wealth, a basic right that man has by his very nature, as was so well emphasized by Pope Pius XII.
Mr. Chairman, I would have many things to add, but I do not want to prolong this debate. But when the Minister of Finance says in the face of the population that the productive function in Canada has nearly reached its limit, I say to him that he did not study his economy, that he is not aware of a productive economy in Canada, in short that he is not aware of the manufacturing function in Canada.
Within two years we can double our national production. By putting everyone to work, all those who do not work now-and we have nearly 50 per cent of the population not working; we still have unemployment pockets, we have citizens of 40, 45, 50 and 60 years of age who could work, but cannot find any work, because there are no jobs for them-in short, if there was a desire to increase production in Canada, a simple solution would be to create jobs, to finance industry, to finance production and also consumption. By so doing, everything would go smoothly. Under the present system, only the production is financed, but we fail to finance consumption. In these times it is consumption that has to be financed first, if production is to reach its objective.
A tight money policy is not the ideal thing in Canada. The ideal procedure for Canadians would be to have credit at their disposal so that they can forge ahead. But, at the present time, our credit is a debt credit. Every dollar in Canada is a debt dollar. And as more money is borrowed, more debts are piled up.
September 9, 1966



That is why a tight money policy is envisaged as well as restrictions in every field, even in all spheres of the national economy. It is unfair and nonsensical to talk about inflation in an affluent country where so many needs are to be satisfied. It is nonsensical to accept such a system in the midst of plenty.
Some people are still starving.

Mr. Chairman, production is good in Canada and it could be better still; yet, in spite of this production, numerous needs are to be satisfied. As I said a moment ago, 12 million citizens have no other income except their low wages; some men, women or children are unemployed and cannot earn any money. There is inflation in Canada at the present time, but there is also deflation, and this is much worse.
A bomb exploded recently in parliament and if this economic problem is not dealt with there will be other bombs exploding, God forbid; I would not want that to happen, but the way this country is run and the way the future of this country is planned will lead to such incidents. We are on the brink of a revolution. The country is prosperous thanks to science and technical know how. The Canadian people know it and want to share in this scientific progress, and we have no right to stop them.

I remind the house, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance made a great to do about the inflationary pressures in our economy in his budget speech last spring. And if there was any value in referring the matter to a parliamentary committee, he should have done it then, so that by now we would have a report from the committee and some facts.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, is not the Minister of Finance playing with this house and with this country. He came in yesterday and spoke as if he knew all the facts, as if he knew precisely what the problems were, as if he had the obvious solutions to those problems. He sets out policies which will have the effect

of cutting important social services and cutting back social capital and doing things which in the opinion of this group, as has been stated eloquently and well by my colleagues, amount to a disservice to the country.
The minister then says to parliament: I want this matter sent to a committee so that I can find out the facts and learn what the trends in the cost of living are, and what factors may have contributed to changes in it in recent months. What was he talking about yesterday if he did not know what those trends are and if he did not know what the factors were? What was the basis of his policies? Perhaps they were based on ignorance of both the trends and the factors involved. Perhaps they were merely traditional policies thrown out without reason and without ground.
I suggest-and I use strong language because I feel strongly about this-that it was a shabby way of dealing with the cost of living of the Canadian people. To bring down a policy, to insist that it is a right policy, to say that all the various circumstances are understood and then to say, in order to be able to make some political speeches across the country, that the question is being sent to a committees for study, is not good enough.
If any investigation of this question should have been made by a parliamentary committee it ought to have been done before the minister produced those policies. In that case those policies might have served the interests of the people of this country rather than doing the opposite, as I feel they do.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I recall the time when the hon. minister brought down his budget, last spring, it was noticeable that it was an American hat, not made to suit the head of Canadians, but for a Canadian head shaped to wear an American hat.
After his last trip to the United States, at the last conference, the minister came back with the price of the hat.

After having the hat adjusted to fit the American head, the minister would fasten the price tag on that hat as furnished by the Americans, and we cannot go to a committee to find out what is wrong. Sometimes I think that with this program we have been given a pretty close shave.
I do not have anything against parliamentary committees, especially when the Secretary of State is the chief witness. We always get amiable answers from her, if not the correct ones. I do not accept that the setting up of this committee will change the situation very much. The minister has set out the government's policy and by the time the committee is in a position to report he may well have put his policies and restrictions into operation as far as possible, so that if the committee does make any recommendations they will come too late, as the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) has stated.
The minister told us yesterday that as long ago as midsummer of last year he began to take precautions. Well, he might have taken even greater precautions and got this committee set up then. We are now in the middle of this inflationary situation. We have the hon. gentleman's own policy to deal with, though at the same time he is asking a committee to 23033-526^

find out what is wrong. If he does not know what is wrong, how can he be sure his policies are correct?
In the circumstances we have little choice, however, and we must let this subject go to a committee for examination.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF TERMS OF REFERENCE TO JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I agree with most of what has been said by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis). Unfortunately, this committee is being set up much too late and the information which it is likely to bring out not necessarily basic to the issue. The underlying reasons for our present difficulties go much deeper and our troubles will never be corrected until financial policies are followed which are very different from those enunciated by the minister last night.
Having said this, I would add that the urgency of a committee study is more acute than it was earlier, simply because as we enter upon centennial year there are problems which are bound to show up within the economy as far as the cost of essential items is concerned; I am thinking of the cost of food. I believe that even at this late stage the work of the committee will be extremely important.
Thus, while in my opinion it would have been far better for this committee to have begun its work much earlier, and though many of the factors which affect the cost of living are beyond the control or range of the committee as they relate to government policy, it is none the less imperative that the committee be assembled at this time, because real urgency attaches to the matter.

One of the reasons there will be further increases in the cost of living is because of the speech the Minister of Finance made yesterday. While he was careful not to forecast the exact type of tax increases that would be made, nevertheless he made it clear that there would be tax increases, and newspapers across Canada today are putting those increases into figures and letting Canadians know that tax increases are coming. It is inevitable that some of the very practices the minister referred to yesterday will continue. People in all sectors of the economy, in all walks of life, will be doing their best to protect themselves against the increased taxes that are coming in the fall, and this is bound to push prices up.
If the Minister of Finance and his government have any measures to cope with the present situation they should be bringing them before parliament now. We should be sitting here next week and we should have those measures before us.
Since I have said a word about what the minister has done in announcing his tax increases I also want to protest against the context in which he announced them. I quote a few words from the minister's speech, as reported at page 8217 of yesterday's Hansard:
When we have before us, perhaps In late October, the measures to authorize the increased revenues made necessary by the income guarantee plan we will be able to review our general fiscal position and consider what changes are desirable in the light of the economic and financial situation.
As a result of that statement it is already being asserted in the press that the reason we are going to have increased taxes is because of what the government calls its income guarantee plan. We all know that that is the phrase which is being applied to the government's proposal to increase old age pensions under the conditions announced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare on July 14.
I remind the Minister of Finance that according to a table on page 2824 of the Canada Gazette, Part I, dated Saturday, August 27, 1966, the taxes that he is taking from the Canadian people for the purpose of

old age security are running on an average of $24 million a month more than is being paid out in old age security. The figures have varied from month to month, but in the month of July the surplus of tax receipts for pensions over the amount paid out was $29.9 million, and for a period of four months the average has been $24 million a month. In other words, there is something in the order of $300 million of a surplus building up in old age security tax receipts in this fiscal year.

Mr. Speaker, we have been through this in various ways a number of times. When the government raised the old age pensions from $65 to $75 a month it said there had to be an increase in taxes, but after being pressed on the point, and having seen fit to lower the eligible age from 70 to 65 on a year-by-year basis, the government then said revenues were more buoyant and it would not be necessary to increase taxes for that purpose.
I submit that the revenues are turning out to be more buoyant than the government itself had anticipated, and that for the immediate future there is no need to increase taxes to pay the kind of pensions the government has in mind.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare on July 14 said that the cost in the initial year of the program he announced that day would be of the order of $225 million. The Minister of Finance is collecting an extra $300 million or more in this fiscal year. Therefore he has no right to say to the Canadian people, as he did yesterday, that one of the reasons, or indeed as some newspapers interpret it, the reason for having to increase taxes is because of the plan to increase pensions.
If the minister wants to raise taxes for some other reason, I think he should be straightforward with us and tell us what that other reason is. It is not for the purpose of pensions, because as I have pointed out, and I have quoted from official government statistics, the amount being collected in sales tax, corporation tax and individual old age security income t?.x in the current fiscal year-and these taxes are collected on an earmarked basis for old age security-is running at an average of $24 million a month more than is being paid out.
September 9, 1966

I do not think it is fair to suggest to the people of Canada that any pittance that is going to be given to the old people on a needs or means test basis is of an amount that requires additional taxation. Therefore I say that instead of this matter being referred to a committee, which will have to study not only price increases which have taken place in recent months but will be confronted with the price increases taking place while it is sitting, we should be staying here dealing with the problems of inflation, our fiscal problems, and above all meeting the emergency needs of our senior citizens.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF TERMS OF REFERENCE TO JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to go over the ground that I covered earlier but I want to repeat that adjourning at this time is a perversion of the responsibilities of parliament to meet a major problem, namely that of inflation. There are also other problems that should be dealt with. Instead of facing the issue the government produces an amendment to a motion giving a committee the power to inquire into and report upon trends in the cost of living in Canada and factors which may have contributed to changes in the cost of living. It is not investigations such as this that are needed at this time; it is action by the government, a government which has no apparent realization of what should be done, how to do it, when to do it, or even whether to do it.
I say no more than that the setting up of this committee is simply political eyewash on the part of the government, and an adjournment at this time-I must join both together-is a gross perversion of the responsibility of parliament to meet a problem that will intensify in the weeks of the adjournment and with regard to which legislation cannot possibly be brought before parliament before the expiry of six weeks.
What is the committee to look into? I thought the Economic Council of Canada had looked into this matter. I thought the minister was the embodiment of all the information that anyone could possibly secure on this subject, with the outstanding staff that he has available. I thought the Bank of Canada had looked into this matter. The minister comes along and says to parliament now: I want to empower a committee to look into the question.
This is nothing but a political dodge designed to give the government extra time to consider a matter with regard to which they
Transportation
have apparently been dormant while it has multiplied and intensified. Of course, we cannot vote against this committee because, after all, committees will meet; but too often the setting up of a committee is nothing but a subterfuge on the part of the government to get away from making any decision or taking any action that has to be taken.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
I conclude by saying that the people of Canada will not be fooled into believing that it is the opposition that makes it impossible for this government to act, and that is one of the major trends and political devices of the government at this time. We are sitting here now; let us act if you have any policies. Up to the present time in this regard you have shown a poverty that is both unseemly and a matter for deep condemnation. As the government postpones further action by another committee, the thief of inflation continues to pick the pockets of Canadians.

In any event I should clarify some of the misconceptions that seem to have arisen in the hon. member's mind on the subject of the adjournment. The house stood adjourned from July 14 until October 5. It was called

back to deal with what I think all hon. members will agree was an emergency situation requiring the immediate and urgent attention of parliament, namely, the stoppage of railway services. speechtext:
As was made evident in the speeches made by hon. members, this latter bill was regarded as an important and urgent matter and it was debated by this house.
At the opening of this emergency session as well as during the proceedings it was made clear that the government's intention was to deal only with the legislation for which the house was assembled. There was also a request made by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition that there should be a day's debate on inflation.
In accordance with that request it was agreed that we sit for one day to discuss inflation, but in point of fact we have discussed it for more than a day and a half. It was a very proper request. Our commitment was kept.
What is being put forward now is a motion on which the house had passed its judgment on July 14. It is only a technicality that requires us to put this motion again. I would point out to the hon. member that in the fight against inflation, as should be clear from the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) last evening, a good many steps must be taken, one of which was the creation of this committee, but many of which require the attention of the government.
I wish to draw the attention of the house to the fact that the International Labour Organization is meeting here next week. It is an important meeting in this period of the development in labour relations, moreover, Canada is the host country. This is a very great honour. The proceedings of this organization are to be opened in this chamber next Monday morning. It is hoped and expected that all the plenary sessions of that meeting will be held in this chamber.
I believe this meeting will continue for about two weeks. Immediately afterward the meeting of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association is to take place. That will be of great interest, I think, to most or all hon. members, and we hope to have hon. members
September 9, 1966

available to take part in those meetings. That cannot be done while the house is sitting.
At present the Prime Minister is attending the Commonwealth Prime Ministers Conference. I think all hon. members will agree that the business before that meeting is of the utmost concern to Canada as a member of the Commonwealth. We have indicated our firm intention, and indeed, our program for the balance of this session. When we adjourned in July the house set October 5 as the date for reconvening. I think it should be very clear to the hon. member that the decision to recess now until October 5 is not only consistent with the earlier action of the house in fixing that particular date, but is the appropriate one having in mind all the circumstances as they exist at the moment. I think hon. members will agree that is a fact.

Now, I am glad to welcome the hon. member back to the house. I hope he will be equally tolerant if 1 myself want to be absent from this place for a few days. I hope he will view my proposals in the kindly light in which I have viewed his return. I hope he will welcome me on October 5 with all the warmth with which I will welcome him on that occasion, when we meet to deal with the second reading of the bank legislation, the medicare bill, and the other important legislation that lies before us.

speechtext:
I wonder if I could say that at least we have a kindly gentleman in the government house leader. I should like to deal, point by point, with the reasons he has given. I believe that there is not one of them that is valid. He spoke of parliament being called back for the purpose of dealing with some particular items. There is no doubt that was the motivation, in the first instance, for parliament having returned. However, in Votes and Proceedings for Monday, August 29, there is set out the following:
Alter consultation with the government, I am satisfied that the public interest requires that the House of Commons, which was adjourned on Thursday, July 14-
Then, the dates are set out, and I continue:
-should meet at an earlier time. In pursuance to the order of the House of Commons passed Thursday, July 14, 1966, I hereby give notice that the House of Commons shall meet on Monday, August 29, 1966, at 2,30 o'clock p.m., and transact its business as if it had been duly adjourned to that time.
Business of the House
The business of the House of Commons is really the business of the people of Canada. There is no indication in there that parliament was returned specifically to deal with two particular items of legislation. The information given by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) to the effect that parliament came back solely to deal with two items is incorrect. The information he gave, that the debate on inflation was an extraordinary arrangement made to suit the convenience or at the request of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), is also incorrect, because these were the normal sitting times of the House of Commons.
Monday will be a normal sitting day as well, and at that time we could carry on with whatever business the government deemed it advisable to call for that time, if it deemed anything to be worthy of the consideration of this house. Reference was made to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) having dealt with the matter of inflation succinctly. This assertion has been pretty well demolished by everyone on the opposition side who took part in the debate, both on the estimates of the Department of Finance and the motion to enlarge the terms of reference of a particular committee, indicating that whatever the Minister of Finance advocated was, in the word of the Leader of the Opposition, "eyewash" and in the words of the representative of this party, "A coverup for complete ineptitude in this field".
The matter of the I.L.O. meeting, of course, is something which undoubtedly was planned some time ago. I am quite sure the delegates from the International Labour Organization will not be inconvenienced if they are asked to sit in the Senate chamber rather than here. Whether or not the senators are there, it is really a vacant place and it should be put to some worth-while use. However, the reference to the I.L.O. conference and the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association conference as reasons why parliament should not meet next week is merely an admission on the part of the government that affairs in other countries are far more important than the affairs of the people of Canada. Even the reference to the Prime Minister being away in London buttresses that sort of reasoning. So far as we are concerned, the affairs of the people of Canada are the important ones with which we should be concerning ourselves. So far as the Prime Minister being absent in London is concerned,-good heavens, we have been carrying on the business of this country

September 9, 1966
Transportation
for the last two and a half years without a Prime Minister. I do not see why we should worry about his presence in London.
All that I can glean from the reasons, spurious and false, which are given by the Minister of Public Works is simply that the government is not prepared to meet parliament and to deal with the affairs of the nation; that it would rather push things to one side for another three or four weeks in hopes that some of these problems will disappear and that in the intervening period they will find something to deal with and present to parliament on October 5. In the light of this sad admission of an absolutely complete bankruptcy by way of program, ideas and legislation on the part of the government, we have no other choice but to adjourn.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY-REJECTION OF SUGGESTION TO HAVE COMMITTEE SIT DURING ADJOURNMENT.
speechtext:
Doubt about the requirement that a committee needs to be granted power to sit while the house is adjourned. There is no doubt that a committee requires authorization by the house to sit while the house is sitting and that a committee has no power to sit after the session is prorogued. But as to what might happen when the house merely recesses, there are two opinions, and I regret to have to say that the better opinion seems to be that the house has to authorize a committee to sit during the period when the house is adjourned.
